Rajab was so named because they used to honor it (*yurajjibunahu*), that is, they glorify it: *rajabtuhu* and *rajjabtuhu*, with light and heavy forms, when you glorify him. Al-Kumayt said:

"I do not seek for myself any protection other than them, nor other than those I revere and glorify."

It was also said: It was so named because fighting is abandoned in it, from the saying of the Arabs: "A man is *arjab* when he is cut off and unable to work."

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "In Paradise there is a river called Rajab, whose water is whiter than snow and sweeter than honey. Whoever fasts one day of Rajab will drink from it." [Fada'il al-Awqat of al-Bayhaqi: 90.]

'Umar said: Sha'ban was so named because the tribes disperse (*yatasha'ab*) in it.

Zayad ibn Maymun narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Sha'ban was so named because much good branches out (*yatashabba*) in it for Ramadan." [17] [Kanz al-'Ummal: 8/591, no. 24293.]

The discussion of Ramadan has already passed. Shawwal was so named because of the *shawlan* of she-camels, the milk-giving ones, lifting their tails in it. [Lisan al-'Arab: 11/377.]

Abu Zayd al-Balkhi said: It was so named because the tribes move (*tashul*) in it, that is, they depart from their places. Dhu al-Qa'da was so named because they sit (*qu'ud*) in it, abstaining from fighting. Dhu al-Hijja was so named because they perform their Hajj in it. God knows best.

Some eloquent speakers said: When the Arabs saw the nobles abandoning their customs and forbidding raids, they called it *Muharram*. When their pillars weakened, their bodies fell ill, and their complexions turned yellow, they called it *Safar*. When the flowers appeared and the gardens bloomed, they called them *Rabi'ani*. When fruits became scarce and water froze, they called them *Jumadiyan*. When the seas stirred, the rivers were hot, and the trees were stripped of leaves, they called it *Rajab*. When virtues became manifest and the tribes branched out, they called it *Sha'ban*. When the *fada* (tamarisk) grew hot and the embers of the *ghada* (saxaul) were extinguished, they called it *Ramadan*. When the clouds cleared, the flies multiplied, and the she-camels lifted their tails, all but those slaughtered, they called it *Shawwal*. When the merchants stopped travelling, they called it *Dhu al-Qa'da*. When they set out for Hajj from every deep valley, showing their chanting and their cries, they called it *Dhu al-Hijja*.

﴿In the Book of God﴾, meaning the Preserved Tablet. It was also said: in His decree, which He decreed ﴿on the day He created the heavens and the earth﴾, ﴿of them four are sacred﴾, the months the Arabs used to glorify, forbidding fighting in them, so that if a man met the slayer of his father or brother, he would not attack him. They are: Rajab, Dhu al-Qa'da, Dhu al-Hijja, and Muharram. One is single and three are consecutive. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 6/39.]

﴿That is the upright religion﴾, the straight reckoning. ﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾, that is, in the sacred months, by doing sin against God, Mighty and Majestic, and abandoning His obedience. Ibn 'Abbas said: It means making fighting and raiding in them lawful. Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Yasar: Do not make what is lawful in them unlawful, nor what is unlawful in them lawful, as the people of polytheism did. Qatada said: Righteous deeds and reward are greater in the sacred months, and sin and wrongdoing in them are greater than wrongdoing in other months, although wrongdoing is always grave. But God magnifies what He wills of His command, just as He chooses from His creation whom He wills.

And fight against the polytheists all together, just as they fight against you all together. Know that Allah is with the God-fearing.

Scholars differed regarding the prohibition of fighting in the sacred months (al-ashhur al-hurum). A group said that it has been abrogated (mansukh). Qatadah and Ata al-Khurasani said: fighting used to be prohibited much in the sacred months, then it was abrogated and fighting in them was made lawful by His saying: ﴿And fight against the polytheists all together﴾, meaning: in them and in other than them.

al-Zuhri said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to forbid fighting in the sacred months, by what Allah the Glorified had revealed of its prohibition, until Surah Bara'ah was revealed, and so fighting the polytheists was made lawful.

Abu Ishaq said: I asked Sufyan al-Thawri about fighting in the sacred month, and he said: This is abrogated, and it has passed; there is no harm in fighting in it or in other than it. They said: Because the Prophet (ﷺ) fought the Hawazin at Hunayn and the Thaqif at al-Ta'if in Shawwal and part of Dhu al-Qa'dah, which indicates that it is abrogated.

Others said: it is not abrogated. Ibn Jurayj said: Ata ibn Abi Rabah swore by Allah that it is not lawful for people to raid in Muharram or in the sacred months, except that they fight in them; and it was not abrogated. Ibn Hayyan said: this verse abrogated every verse that contains a concession.

﴿Indeed, the postponement (al-nasi')﴾: al-Hasan, Alqamah, Qatadah, Mujahid, Nafi' (other than Warsh), Abu Amir, Isa, al-A'mash, Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Amir read al-nasi' with a long vowel and a hamzah, and this was chosen by Abu Ubaydah and Abu Hatim. It is a verbal noun (masdar) like al-kharir, al-si'ir and al-hariq and the like; it could also be a passive form shifted to the pattern fa'il like al-jarih, al-qatil and al-ghariq, its implied meaning being: the postponed month. Abu Abd al-Rahman, Talhah, al-Ashhab and Shibl read (al-nasu') with a sukun on the sin and a hamzah, as a masdar only. Abu Amr and Warsh [Warsh: he is Abu Sa'id, and Abu Amr Uthman ibn Sa'id ibn Abd Allah ibn Amr] read al-nasiyy with shaddah and without hamzah.

This was narrated from Ibn Kathir, meaning al-nasiyy, i.e. the abandoned, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾, from forgetting. It may be that its origin is the hamzah, lightened. They differed about the root of the word. al-Akhfash said: it is from postponement, and from it comes al-nasi'ah in sale; it is said: Allah postponed (anså) his term, and he postponed (nasa'a) in his term, i.e., delayed it. Qutrub said: it is from increase; every increase that occurs in something is nasi', and likewise it is said of milk when it is increased with water: nasi' and nasu', and of a pregnant woman: nasu'at, due to the addition of the waw in it. And "I postponed the she-camel (nasa'at al-naqah) and made her go (anse'tuha)" when you drive her so that her pace increases. Qatadah said: some people of the people of error made an agreement, and they added Safar to the sacred months. A man would stand at the season (al-mawsim) and say: Behold, your gods have made Muharram forbidden, so they would forbid it that year; then he would stand the following year and say: Behold, your gods have made Safar forbidden, so they would forbid it that year. And these two were called: the two Safars.

As for the meaning of the nasi' and the beginning of its matter, as the scholars have related it in different wordings but with one agreed meaning: the Arabs used to forbid the four months, and this was among the things they held to from the religion of Abraham the Friend and his son Ishmael. The Arabs were people of wars and raids, and it was hard for them to remain three consecutive months without raiding in them. They said: If three sacred months follow one another for us, in which we gain nothing, we will surely go hungry, for we gain only on the backs of our animals. So they would sometimes need, along with that, to make lawful the forbidden month, or another of the sacred months, due to a war that occurs between them; they would dislike making it lawful and would make lawful the forbidden month.

They would continue this for a time: they forbid Safar, meaning Muharram, and they say: it is one of the two Safars. Some people have interpreted the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no Safar" in this light. Then they would also need to postpone Safar to the month after it, as they needed to postpone Muharram; so they postpone its prohibition to Rabi'. Then they would continue in this as long as Allah willed, then they would need the same again, and so on, so the prohibition keeps shifting from month to month until the prohibition circled through the entire year. Then Islam came when Muharram had returned to its original place which Allah the Mighty and Majestic had set, and that was after a long time.

Mujahid said: The polytheists would perform Hajj in each month for two years. So they performed Hajj in Dhu al-Hijjah for two years, then they performed Hajj in Muharram for two years, then they performed Hajj in Safar for two years. Likewise, in the months that coincided with the Hajj of Abu Bakr, which he performed before the Farewell Hajj, in the second year, in Dhu al-Qa'dah; then the Prophet (ﷺ) performed the Farewell Hajj in the following year, and it coincided with Dhu al-Hijjah. That is when the Prophet (ﷺ) said in his sermon: "Behold, time has returned to the form in which it was on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth. The number of months is twelve, of which four are sacred: three consecutive, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and Muharram, and Rajab, which lies between Jumada and Sha'ban." [18] [Musnad Ahmad: 5/37.]

He (ﷺ) meant that the sacred months had returned to their places, the Hajj had returned to Dhu al-Hijjah, and the nasi' was abolished.

They differed about who first practised the nasi'. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: The first to practise the nasi' were the Banu Malik ibn Kinanah, and there was Abu Thumamah Ubadah ibn Awf ibn Umayyah al-Kinani, who would attend the season every year on a donkey and say: O people, I speak and I am not afraid, and what I say cannot be turned back. We have made Muharram forbidden and postponed Safar; then the following year he would say: We have made Safar forbidden and postponed Muharram.

al-Kalbi said: The first to do that was a man from Kinanah called Nu'aym ibn Tha'labah, who would be ahead of people at the season, and when people resolved to depart, he would stand and address the people, saying: There is no turning back of what I have decreed; I am the one who is not ghā'ib and not disappointed. The polytheists would say to him: Labbayk! Then he would ask them to postpone for him a month in which they would make a change, and he would say: Indeed, general fighting is forbidden. When he said that, they unstrung their bows, broke their spearheads and sheaths, and if he said: It is lawful, they tied their bows, strengthened their sheaths, and raided the people.

[And it is said, after] Nu'aym ibn Tha'labah, a man called Junadah ibn Awf, who is the one whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) encountered.

Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas that the first to practise the nasi' was Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Ba'lathah ibn Khindif. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: he was a man of Banu Kinanah called al-Qalmas in the Jahiliyyah. The people of the Jahiliyyah did not raid one another in the sacred months; a man would meet the killer of his father or brother and not be touched; then one of them would say: Let us go out. He would be told: This is Muharram. Al-Qalmas would say: I have postponed it this year, so two Safars; and when the following year comes, we will decide and make them both forbidden. [............] [A torn passage in the original.] al-Kumayt said:

Are we not the postponers over Mudar, making the months of lawfulness forbidden?

[Lisan al-Arab: 1/167.]

That is the nasi' of which Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the postponement is an increase in disbelief, by which those who disbelieve are led astray﴾. The people of Medina, Asim and Abu Amr read yudallu with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the dad, and Abu Hatim chose it because the misguided are joined to it, for His saying: ﴿by which those who disbelieve are led astray, they make it lawful one year and forbid it another year﴾. Abu Raja', al-Hasan, Abu Abd al-Rahman, Qatadah, Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin read yadillu with a kasra on the dad, and it has two aspects: one is that alladhina kafaru is in the accusative position, meaning Allah leads astray by it those who disbelieve. The second aspect is that alladhina is in the nominative position, meaning those who disbelieve are led astray by it, that is, the misguided among them. The people of Kufa read yuddallu with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the dad, which is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and the choice of Abu Ubaydah, for His saying: ﴿Made attractive to them is the evil of their deeds﴾. They make it lawful, meaning the nasi', one year, and forbid it another year, ﴿to make conform﴾, i.e., to agree with, ﴿Ibn Abbas said: to resemble.﴾ The historian said: it means that they would not make lawful a month of the sacred months without forbidding in its place a month of the lawful months, and would not forbid a month of the lawful months without making lawful in its place a month of the sacred months, so that the sacred months would not exceed four months of what Allah had forbidden, thereby matching the number. That is what is meant.

﴿So that they make lawful what Allah has forbidden. The evil of their deeds has been made attractive to them. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾

O you who believe, what is [the matter with] you that, when it is said to you, "Go forth in the way of God," you grow heavy toward the earth? ﴿O you who believe, what is wrong with you, that when you are told, "Go forth in the cause of God," you cling heavily to the earth?﴾

This verse contains an exhortation from God, glorified is He, to the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to campaign at Tabuk. The reason is that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) returned from al-Ta'if, he ordered jihad for the expedition against the Romans. This was at a time of hardship for the people, drought in the land, and intense heat, when the palm trees were being scorched and the fruits had ripened. The campaign against the Romans weighed heavily on the people. They loved shade and remaining in their homes and with their wealth, so going out to fight was hard for them. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) rarely went out on an expedition without alluding to it and concealing it by mentioning something else, except for the expedition of Tabuk, because of the great distance and the large number of the enemy. He did this so that the people could prepare, and he commanded them to fight and informed them of what he intended.

When God knew that the people were reluctant, God, exalted is He, sent down: ﴿O you who believe, what is [the matter with] you?﴾, meaning, what has commanded you? ﴿When it is said to you, "Go forth,"﴾ that is, when the Messenger of God says to you, ﴿Go forth in the way of God﴾, meaning, set out. The root of nafr (going forth) is leaving one place for another because of a matter that has arisen. It is said: "So-and-so went forth (nafara) to a frontier post of such-and-such," he goes forth (yanfuru) nafran and nufuran. From it comes the nufur (bolting) and nifar (shying) of a beast. ﴿You cling heavily (ithaqaltum)﴾ means you were slow.

Al-Mubarrad said: ﴿You inclined to the earth (akhlattum ila al-ard)﴾, meaning you stayed in your land and your dwellings. Its original form is tathaqaltum, and the ta' was assimilated into the tha' (idgham), and an alif was added to make it possible to begin the word with it, as in His saying: ﴿until, when they had all overtaken one another therein﴾ [Surah al-A'raf 7:38]. Al-'Ala' and al-Kisa'i read "iṭṭayyarnā" and "irjafat" (as in the reports about omens) [in the sense of ill omens].

The poet says:
"He lifts the din when he longs for it, green,
Sweet of taste when he follows (ittaba'a) one after another (al-qubal)."

That is, when it follows in succession (tatabba'a).

﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ That is, are you content with this world and abandon the bliss and reward of the Hereafter in exchange? ﴿Then the enjoyment of the life of this world, in comparison with the Hereafter, is but little.﴾ Then He threatened them for abandoning jihad: ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾ in the Hereafter. It was also said that this refers to the withholding of rain from them. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read "tunfirū" with a damma on the fa', and both are two dialectal forms.

Najda ibn Nufay' was asked about this verse from Ibn ʿAbbas, and he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) called upon a tribe from among the tribes of the Arabs to go forth, but they were reluctant, so the rain was withheld from them, and that was their punishment. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 10/174.]

﴿And He will replace you with another people﴾, better than you and more obedient. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They are the sons of Persia. Abu Salih said: They are the people of Yemen. ﴿And you will not harm Him at all by abandoning the going forth.﴾ ﴿And God is over all things Competent.﴾ ﴿If you do not support him, God has already supported him.﴾ This is a declaration from God that He Himself undertakes the support of His Messenger and the manifestation of His religion, whether they help him or not, and that He has already supported him when his allies were few and his enemies many. How much more so today, when he is in great number and equipment. Therefore, He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿If you do not go forth, O believers, when he calls you to go forth, and do not support him when he asks you for support, then God will help him and will compensate him for you, as He supported him﴾ ﴿when those who disbelieved expelled him.﴾

It was also said: [the meaning is] if you do not support him, God has already supported him ﴿when those who disbelieved expelled him﴾ from Mecca, when they plotted against him, intended to expel him, and resolved to kill him. ﴿The second of two﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), and he was one of the two; the two were the Messenger of God and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. ﴿When they were both in the cave﴾, which is a cavity in a mountain in Mecca called Thawr. ﴿When he said to his companion, Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, "Do not grieve; indeed God is with us,"﴾ for aid and support. The grief of Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, was not cowardice nor an ill opinion of God, but rather concern for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). This is shown by his saying: "O Messenger of God, if you are killed, I am only one man; but if you are killed, the nation is destroyed."

Hammam reported from Thabit from Anas that Abu Bakr told him: I said to the Prophet (ﷺ) while we were in the cave: "If anyone looked down at his feet, he would see us." He said: "O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two whom God is the third of?"

Mujahid said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) remained in the cave for three days.

ʿUrwa said: Abu Bakr had a loan of a flock of sheep, and ʿAmir ibn Fuhayra would bring those sheep to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the cave.

Qatada said: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr would visit them secretly. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wanted to leave, he summoned them, and they were four: the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, ʿAmir ibn Fuhayra, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Uraiqit al-Laythi.

al-Zuhri said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr entered the cave, God sent a pair of doves, which laid eggs at the bottom of the cavity, and a spider, which wove a web. When Suraqa ibn Malik came in pursuit of them and saw the doves' eggs and the spider's web, he said: "If they had entered it, the eggs would have been broken and the spider's web torn," so he turned back.

The Prophet said: "O God, blind their eyes," so their eyes were blinded from seeing the entrance, and they began to strike to the right and left around the cave.

al-Sari ibn Yahya reported from Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: Some men mentioned during the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, as though they preferred ʿUmar over Abu Bakr. He said: This reached ʿUmar, and he said: "By God, one night of Abu Bakr is better than the family of ʿUmar, and one day of Abu Bakr is better than the family of ʿUmar. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out one night, setting off for the cave, and Abu Bakr was with him. He began walking, sometimes in front of him and sometimes behind him, until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) reached him and said: 'O Abu Bakr, what is the matter with you? You walk sometimes in front of me and sometimes behind me.' He said: 'O Messenger of God, I remember the pursuers, so I walk behind you; then I remember the ambush, so I walk in front of you.' He said: 'O Abu Bakr, would you have wished that something should happen to you instead of me?' He said: 'Yes, by the One who sent you with truth.'"

When they came to the cave, Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, said: "Stay where you are, O Messenger of God, until I search the cave." He entered and searched it, and when he reached the top, he remembered that he had not searched the stone, so he said: "Stay where you are, O Messenger of God, until I search the stone." He entered and searched, then said: "Come down, O Messenger of God," and he came down. ʿUmar said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, that night was better than the family of ʿUmar." [Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya: 3/221.]

Abu ʿAwana reported from Firas from al-Sha'bi who said: God rebuked all the people of the earth in this verse except Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him. Abu Bakr said:

"The Prophet said, and he did not panic, honoring me,
While we were in the distress of the darkness of the cave.
Do not fear anything, for God is our third,
And He has undertaken for me the manifestation [of victory].
The plot of one whose hostility you fear
Is only the plot of the devils, which they plotted for the disbelievers.
God will destroy them all for what they earned,
And will make their end into the Fire."
[Siyar al-Huda wa'l-Rashad: 3/349, which mentions the rest of the verses. Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya: 3/224, which mentions only the first two verses, and in it: "We were in a sadf of the darkness of the cave."]

﴿Then God sent down His tranquility (sakinatahu)﴾, that is, His calm and assurance, ﴿upon him﴾, that is, upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Ibn ʿAbbas said: upon Abu Bakr. As for the Prophet (ﷺ), tranquility was upon him before that. ﴿And strengthened him (wa-ayyadahu)﴾. Mujahid read "wa-āyadahu" with a long vowel. ﴿With soldiers you did not see﴾, namely the angels. ﴿And He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest﴾, that is, the humbled and defeated. ﴿And the word of God is the highest﴾. The word "kalimatu" is nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. Ya'qub read "wa-kalimata Allah" in the accusative by coordination (ʿatf). ﴿It is the highest﴾, the exalted.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: The lowest word is the word of polytheism, and the highest is "There is no god but God." ﴿And God is Mighty and Wise.﴾

﴿Go forth, light and heavy (khifafan wa-thiqalan)﴾. Abu al-Duha said: This was the first verse of Bara'a (al-Tawba) to be revealed. Muqatil said: They said: "Among us are the heavy (laden), the one with dependents and property, the one whose affairs are preoccupied, and the one who is busy." So God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse and refused to excuse them.

They differed about the meaning of khifaf and thiqal. Anas, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, Qatada, ʿIkrima, Shamir ibn ʿAtiyya and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "Busy and occupied." al-Hakam said: "Busy and not busy." al-Hasan [said]: "Busy." Abu Salih said: "Light (khifafan) in wealth, that is, poor, and heavy (thiqalan) in it, that is, rich." Ibn Zayd said: "The heavy is the one who has property, so he is heavy because he has property, which is greater than the light one who has no property." He said: "Energetic and not energetic." ʿAtiyya al-ʿAwfi said: "Riding and on foot." Murra al-Hamadhani said: "Healthy and sick." Yaman ibn Rabab said: "Single and married."

It was also said: "Light (khifafan), hastening, not going out except at the moment of the call to go forth"; he says: "The man became light (khafa), i.e., he walked hastily." "Heavy (thiqalan)," that is, after preparing and equipping oneself for it.

It was also said: "Light (khifafan) in weapons, that is, having few of them, and heavy (thiqalan), having many of them," for the Arabs call the unarmed man "light" (mukhaff).

It was also said: "Light (khifafan) in your livestock and children, and heavy (thiqalan) with many of them." ﴿And strive with your wealth and your selves in the way of God. That is better for you, if you only knew.﴾

ʿAli ibn Zayd reported from Anas that Abu Talha recited Surat Bara'a, and when he came to this verse, ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾, he said: "O my sons, equip me, equip me!" His sons said: "May God have mercy on you; you fought with the Prophet (ﷺ) until he died, and with Abu Bakr and ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them, until they died. So we will fight on your behalf." He said: "Equip me!" So he went out to sea, and he died at sea, and they could not find an island to bury him in until after seven days, and they buried him there, and he had not changed. [See Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/155.]

al-Zuhri said: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab went out to the expedition when one of his eyes had been lost. It was said to him: "You are sick, one afflicted with harm." He said: "Let the light and the heavy go forth. If I am unable to fight, I will increase the number and guard the baggage."

O you who believe, what is [the matter with] you that, when it is said to you, "Go forth in the way of God," you grow heavy toward the earth? ﴿O you who believe, what is wrong with you, that when you are told, "Go forth in the cause of God," you cling heavily to the earth?﴾

This verse contains an exhortation from God, glorified is He, to the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to campaign at Tabuk. The reason is that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) returned from al-Ta'if, he ordered jihad for the expedition against the Romans. This was at a time of hardship for the people, drought in the land, and intense heat, when the palm trees were being scorched and the fruits had ripened. The campaign against the Romans weighed heavily on the people. They loved shade and remaining in their homes and with their wealth, so going out to fight was hard for them. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) rarely went out on an expedition without alluding to it and concealing it by mentioning something else, except for the expedition of Tabuk, because of the great distance and the large number of the enemy. He did this so that the people could prepare, and he commanded them to fight and informed them of what he intended.

When God knew that the people were reluctant, God, exalted is He, sent down: ﴿O you who believe, what is [the matter with] you?﴾, meaning, what has commanded you? ﴿When it is said to you, "Go forth,"﴾ that is, when the Messenger of God says to you, ﴿Go forth in the way of God﴾, meaning, set out. The root of nafr (going forth) is leaving one place for another because of a matter that has arisen. It is said: "So-and-so went forth (nafara) to a frontier post of such-and-such," he goes forth (yanfuru) nafran and nufuran. From it comes the nufur (bolting) and nifar (shying) of a beast. ﴿You cling heavily (ithaqaltum)﴾ means you were slow.

Al-Mubarrad said: ﴿You inclined to the earth (akhlattum ila al-ard)﴾, meaning you stayed in your land and your dwellings. Its original form is tathaqaltum, and the ta' was assimilated into the tha' (idgham), and an alif was added to make it possible to begin the word with it, as in His saying: ﴿until, when they had all overtaken one another therein﴾ [Surah al-A'raf 7:38]. Al-'Ala' and al-Kisa'i read "iṭṭayyarnā" and "irjafat" (as in the reports about omens) [in the sense of ill omens].

The poet says:
"He lifts the din when he longs for it, green,
Sweet of taste when he follows (ittaba'a) one after another (al-qubal)."

That is, when it follows in succession (tatabba'a).

﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ That is, are you content with this world and abandon the bliss and reward of the Hereafter in exchange? ﴿Then the enjoyment of the life of this world, in comparison with the Hereafter, is but little.﴾ Then He threatened them for abandoning jihad: ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾ in the Hereafter. It was also said that this refers to the withholding of rain from them. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read "tunfirū" with a damma on the fa', and both are two dialectal forms.

Najda ibn Nufay' was asked about this verse from Ibn ʿAbbas, and he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) called upon a tribe from among the tribes of the Arabs to go forth, but they were reluctant, so the rain was withheld from them, and that was their punishment. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 10/174.]

﴿And He will replace you with another people﴾, better than you and more obedient. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They are the sons of Persia. Abu Salih said: They are the people of Yemen. ﴿And you will not harm Him at all by abandoning the going forth.﴾ ﴿And God is over all things Competent.﴾ ﴿If you do not support him, God has already supported him.﴾ This is a declaration from God that He Himself undertakes the support of His Messenger and the manifestation of His religion, whether they help him or not, and that He has already supported him when his allies were few and his enemies many. How much more so today, when he is in great number and equipment. Therefore, He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿If you do not go forth, O believers, when he calls you to go forth, and do not support him when he asks you for support, then God will help him and will compensate him for you, as He supported him﴾ ﴿when those who disbelieved expelled him.﴾

He said: This reached ʿUmar, and he said: "By God, one night of Abu Bakr is better than the family of ʿUmar, and one day of Abu Bakr is better than the family of ʿUmar. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out one night, setting off for the cave, and Abu Bakr was with him. He began walking, sometimes in front of him and sometimes behind him, until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) reached him and said: 'O Abu Bakr, what is the matter with you? You walk sometimes in front of me and sometimes behind me.' He said: 'O Messenger of God, I remember the pursuers, so I walk behind you; then I remember the ambush, so I walk in front of you.' He said: 'O Abu Bakr, would you have wished that something should happen to you instead of me?' He said: 'Yes, by the One who sent you with truth.'"

When they came to the cave, Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, said: "Stay where you are, O Messenger of God, until I search the cave." He entered and searched it, and when he reached the top, he remembered that he had not searched the stone, so he said: "Stay where you are, O Messenger of God, until I search the stone." He entered and searched, then said: "Come down, O Messenger of God," and he came down. ʿUmar said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, that night was better than the family of ʿUmar." [Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya: 3/221.]

Abu ʿAwana reported from Firas from al-Sha'bi who said: God rebuked all the people of the earth in this verse except Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him. Abu Bakr said:

"The Prophet said, and he did not panic, honoring me,
While we were in the distress of the darkness of the cave.
Do not fear anything, for God is our third,
And He has undertaken for me the manifestation [of victory].
The plot of one whose hostility you fear
Is only the plot of the devils, which they plotted for the disbelievers.
God will destroy them all for what they earned,
And will make their end into the Fire."
[Siyar al-Huda wa'l-Rashad: 3/349, which mentions the rest of the verses. Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya: 3/224, which mentions only the first two verses, and in it: "We were in a sadf of the darkness of the cave."]

﴿Then God sent down His tranquility (sakinatahu)﴾, that is, His calm and assurance, ﴿upon him﴾, that is, upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Ibn ʿAbbas said: upon Abu Bakr. As for the Prophet (ﷺ), tranquility was upon him before that. ﴿And strengthened him (wa-ayyadahu)﴾. Mujahid read "wa-āyadahu" with a long vowel. ﴿With soldiers you did not see﴾, namely the angels. ﴿And He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest﴾, that is, the humbled and defeated. ﴿And the word of God is the highest﴾. The word "kalimatu" is nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. Ya'qub read "wa-kalimata Allah" in the accusative by coordination (ʿatf). ﴿It is the highest﴾, the exalted.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: The lowest word is the word of polytheism, and the highest is "There is no god but God." ﴿And God is Mighty and Wise.﴾

﴿Go forth, light and heavy (khifafan wa-thiqalan)﴾. Abu al-Duha said: This was the first verse of Bara'a (al-Tawba) to be revealed. Muqatil said: They said: "Among us are the heavy (laden), the one with dependents and property, the one whose affairs are preoccupied, and the one who is busy." So God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse and refused to excuse them.

They differed about the meaning of khifaf and thiqal. Anas, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, Qatada, ʿIkrima, Shamir ibn ʿAtiyya and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "Busy and occupied." al-Hakam said: "Busy and not busy." al-Hasan [said]: "Busy." Abu Salih said: "Light (khifafan) in wealth, that is, poor, and heavy (thiqalan) in it, that is, rich." Ibn Zayd said: "The heavy is the one who has property, so he is heavy because he has property, which is greater than the light one who has no property." He said: "Energetic and not energetic." ʿAtiyya al-ʿAwfi said: "Riding and on foot." Murra al-Hamadhani said: "Healthy and sick." Yaman ibn Rabab said: "Single and married."

It was also said: "Light (khifafan), hastening, not going out except at the moment of the call to go forth"; he says: "The man became light (khafa), i.e., he walked hastily." "Heavy (thiqalan)," that is, after preparing and equipping oneself for it.

It was also said: "Light (khifafan) in weapons, that is, having few of them, and heavy (thiqalan), having many of them," for the Arabs call the unarmed man "light" (mukhaff).

It was also said: "Light (khifafan) in your livestock and children, and heavy (thiqalan) with many of them." ﴿And strive with your wealth and your selves in the way of God. That is better for you, if you only knew.﴾

ʿAli ibn Zayd reported from Anas that Abu Talha recited Surat Bara'a, and when he came to this verse, ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾, he said: "O my sons, equip me, equip me!" His sons said: "May God have mercy on you; you fought with the Prophet (ﷺ) until he died, and with Abu Bakr and ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them, until they died. So we will fight on your behalf." He said: "Equip me!" So he went out to sea, and he died at sea, and they could not find an island to bury him in until after seven days, and they buried him there, and he had not changed. [See Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/155.]

al-Zuhri said: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab went out to the expedition when one of his eyes had been lost. It was said to him: "You are sick, one afflicted with harm." He said: "Let the light and the heavy go forth. If I am unable to fight, I will increase the number and guard the baggage."

Then there was revealed concerning those hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk: ﴿If it had been a near advantage and a moderate journey, they would have followed you.﴾ The pronoun in "kāna" (it was) is implicit; meaning: if what they were being called to were a near gain, an immediate booty, and a journey of moderate distance and a nearby destination.

Al-Mubarrad said: "qāṣidan" means "having an aim," like tāmir and labin (i.e., possessing dates and milk). It was also said that it is a road that is intended, so its attribute was put in the form fā'ila in the sense of maf'ūla, as in His saying ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ [Surah al-Haqqah: 21], meaning "pleasing." ﴿But the distance seemed long to them.﴾ That is, the journey. Al-Kisa'i said: it is the military expedition to which they go out. Qutrub said: it is a far journey, and it was called shuqqah because it burdens (tashuqqu) a person. The reading is with a damma on the shīn, which is the prevalent dialect; ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read it with a kasra on the shīn, which is the dialect of Qays.

﴿They will swear by Allah, "If we had been able, we would have gone out with you."﴾ Al-A'mash read the wāw with a damma, because the original vowel of the wāw is a damma; al-Hasan read it with a fatha, because the fatha is the lightest of the vowels; the rest read it with a kasra, because the jussive is moved with a kasra (i.e., the vowel of the waw of the plural is kasra in this context, following the rule of the sound of the verb's ending). ﴿They destroy themselves,﴾ by the false oath. ﴿And Allah knows that they are liars﴾ in their oaths [and their excuses]. ﴿May Allah pardon you.﴾ He placed the pardon before the mention of the killing (i.e., the stern words).

Qatadah and ʿAmr ibn Maymun said: "Two things the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did, for which he had not been commanded: his permission given to the hypocrites, and his taking ransom from the captives. So Allah rebuked him, as you hear."

Some of them said: Allah, mighty and majestic, honoured him and elevated his station, [so this is an opening of speech with a supplication for him], as a man says to one he addresses, if he is dear to him: "May Allah pardon you for what you did regarding my need, and may Allah be pleased with you, unless you visit me." It was also said: its meaning is, "May Allah perpetuate pardon for you."

﴿Why did you give them permission until it became clear to you who were truthful in their excuses and you knew the liars among them?﴾ ﴿Those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not ask your permission (to stay away from striving with their wealth and lives)...﴾ up to His saying, ﴿and their hearts are in doubt﴾: they doubted and the hearts of them were hypocritical. ﴿So they are in their doubt, wavering,﴾ bewildered. ﴿And if they had intended to go out to the campaign, they would have prepared for it an equipment,﴾ which is provisions and mounts. ﴿But Allah disliked their being sent forth [i.e., their going out], so He held them back and restrained them.﴾ ﴿And it was said, "Remain with those who remain [behind]":﴾ meaning the sick and the disabled. It was also said: the women and the children.

﴿Had they gone out among you...﴾ the verse. This was because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded the people to strive for the expedition to Tabuk. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out with his army, he and his host, at the Thaniyyat al-Wada', and it was not the smaller of the two armies, then when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ marched, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy stayed behind, along with those hypocrites and people of doubt who stayed behind. So Allah, exalted, revealed [consoling] His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Had they gone out among you﴾, meaning the hypocrites, ﴿they would have added to you nothing but corruption﴾, meaning mischief. Al-Kalbi said: evil; it was also said: treachery and deception. ﴿And they would have hurried through your ranks﴾, meaning: they would have urged their mounts between you. It is said: the she-camel "waḍaʿat, taḍaʿu, waḍūʿan" when she hastened her pace, and "awḍaʿahā īḍāʿan" meaning he exerted her and made her hasten. The rajaz poet said:

"Would that I were in it as a young camel, / hastening in it and galloping."

And he said: "Desist, for you have often / hastened in its haste."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: it means they would have hastened flight amidst your midst. The root of khilāl is from khalal, which is a gap between two things, and between people in rows and other things. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Align your rows; let not Satan cut through you, like young sheep of the hadhf [i.e., herd]." (al-Mu'jam al-Saghir of al-Tabarani.)

﴿Seeking to cause you discord﴾: that is, seeking for you, saying: they seek for you what you may be tested with, saying: "The enemy has gathered against you such-and-such," causing you harm.

Al-Kalbi said: ﴿seeking to cause you discord﴾ means the unseen and the secret. al-Dahhak said: it means disbelief. It is said of it: "baghaytuhu abghīhi bughā'an" when you seek it, in the sense of "baghaytu lahu" (I sought for him). Similar is "ʿakamtuka" (I hindered you) when I hindered for you in it; and when they wanted to trouble you with it, they said: "abghaytuka, aḥlabtuka, a'kamtuka."

﴿And among you are listeners for them﴾: Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: there are spies among you for them, who convey to them what they hear from you. Qatadah and Ibn Yasar said: among you is one who listens to their speech and follows them. ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴿

﴿Certainly they had sought discord before, and they turned matters over in their minds against you﴾: that is, they worked for it to turn your companions away from the religion and return them to disbelief by discouraging people from you before this day, like the deed of ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy on the day of Uhud, when he turned away from you with his companions. ﴿And they contrived against you affairs,﴾ they deliberated concerning you and concerning the nullifying of your religion, by discouraging people from you and scattering your companions.

﴿Until the truth came,﴾ that is, victory and triumph, ﴿and the command of Allah became manifest,﴾ the religion of Allah, ﴿while they were averse.﴾ ﴿And among them is he who says, "Give me permission and do not put me to trial." ...﴾ the verse.

It was revealed concerning Jadd ibn Qays, the hypocrite. This was because when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prepared for the expedition to Tabuk, he said to him: "O Abu Wahb, would you like to fight the sons of al-Asfar (the Byzantines) and take from them some women of beauty?" It was said: he was commanded with this because the Abyssinians had overcome a region of the Romans and had begotten daughters who were a mixture of Roman whiteness and Abyssinian blackness, so they were yellow-lipped (ṣafr al-luʿas). [Al-luʿs: the blackness of the gums and lip; it was also said: a blackness in the lip; and it was said: a blackness that covers the lip of a fair woman.] When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that to him, Jadd said: "O Messenger of Allah, you know my people: I am a man greatly fond of women, and I fear that if I see the daughters of al-Asfar I will not be patient with them. So do not put me to trial with them, grant me permission to stay behind, and I will assist you with my wealth." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned away from him and said: "I have granted you permission." So Allah revealed: ﴿And among them (i.e., the hypocrites) is he who says, "Give me permission" (to stay behind) ﴾ ﴿"and do not put me to trial" with the daughters of al-Asfar.﴾ [Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari.]

Qatadah said: "and do not leave me to my own devices." ﴿Surely they have fallen into trial itself﴾: they fell into sin and polytheism, having incurred by their treachery and their opposition to the command of Allah and His Messenger. ﴿And indeed Hell encompasses the disbelievers﴾: surrounding them and gathering them within it.

When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the Banu Salamah, of whom [Jadd] was one: "Who is your leader?" They said: "Jadd ibn Qays, except that he is emaciated and a coward." The Prophet ﷺ said: "And what disease is more grievous than stinginess? Rather, your leader is the fair-skinned, curly-haired youth, Bishr ibn al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur." Hassan said concerning him:

"The Messenger of Allah said, and speech is binding, / concerning one of us whom you consider a leader.
We said to him: 'Jadd ibn Qays, though with the stinginess / that is imputed to him among us, though he be most wretched.'
He said: 'And what disease is more grievous than the one / you have accused him of? A rounded one with a hand (of wealth)...'
And Bishr ibn al-Bara' was made leader for his generosity, / and it is right that Bishr, possessor of bounty, be made leader.
When the delegation came to him, he would plunder his wealth, / and say: 'Take him, for he will be a returner tomorrow.'"

And he said: "Desist, for you have often / hastened in its haste."

From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Align your rows; let not Satan cut through you, like young sheep of the hadhf [i.e., herd]." (al-Mu'jam al-Saghir of al-Tabarani.)

Similar is "ʿakamtuka" (I hindered you) when I hindered for you in it; and when they wanted to trouble you with it, they said: "abghaytuka, aḥlabtuka, a'kamtuka."

It was revealed concerning Jadd ibn Qays, the hypocrite. This was because when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prepared for the expedition to Tabuk, he said to him: "O Abu Wahb, would you like to fight the sons of al-Asfar (the Byzantines) and take from them some women of beauty?" It was said: he was commanded with this because the Abyssinians had overcome a region of the Romans and had begotten daughters who were a mixture of Roman whiteness and Abyssinian blackness, so they were yellow-lipped (ṣafr al-luʿas). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned away from him and said: "I have granted you permission." He said: 'And what disease is more grievous than the one / you have accused him of? A rounded one with a hand (of wealth)...'
And Bishr ibn al-Bara' was made leader for his generosity, / and it is right that Bishr, possessor of bounty, be made leader.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 9, verse 50–59:

﴿If good befalls you, it grieves them,﴾ [meaning] the hypocrites; ﴿and if a calamity strikes you, they say, "We had already taken our precaution," meaning, we had made our excuse and resolved to sit back and abandon the raid, ﴿before this [calamity]﴾, before this misfortune.

﴿Say, "Nothing will befall us except what Allah has decreed for us,"﴾ say to them, O Muhammad. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "Say, 'Will anything befall us?'" and Talha ibn Musarrif recited it this way. ﴿except what Allah has written for us in the Preserved Tablet, and then decreed upon us. He is our Protector (mawla), our Guardian, our Helper and our Keeper.﴾ Al-Kalbi said: He is more deserving of us than ourselves, in death and in life. ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ ﴿Say, "Do you await for us anything but one of the two best outcomes?"﴾ Those being victory and conquest together with a great reward, or death as a martyr, in which is the great triumph.

Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi informed us, saying: Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Adl narrated to us; Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-'Abdi narrated to us; Abu Bakr Umayya ibn Bistam narrated to us; Yazid ibn Bazi' informed us, from Bakr ibn al-Qasim, from Suhayl, from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah guarantees to whoever goes out in His cause, with no motive for going out except belief in Allah and confirmation of His Messenger, that He will grant him martyrdom, or return him to his family forgiven, with whatever reward and spoils he has gained."

﴿And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Himself,﴾ so that Allah destroys them as He destroyed the earlier nations. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning thunderbolts. Ibn Jurayj said: meaning death, or punishment by slaying at our hands, as it befell the nations before us. ﴿So await,﴾ their destruction, ﴿indeed we are waiting along with you.﴾ Al-Hasan said: ﴿So await﴾ means the promises of Satan; ﴿indeed we are waiting along with you﴾ means the promises of Allah concerning the manifestation of His religion and the uprooting of those who oppose it. Satan used to hold out to them the hope of the death of the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿Say, "Spend willingly or unwillingly; it will never be accepted from you."﴾ It was revealed concerning Jadd ibn Qays when he asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to stay behind from the campaign, saying: "This is my wealth, I will help you with it." The apparent form of the verse is an imperative, but its meaning is a statement and a condition, its implied sense being: if you spend willingly or unwillingly, it will not be accepted from you, like the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them﴾ (the verse). The poet said:

Treat us harshly or kindly, there is no blame upon us,
nor are we disdained, should you turn away.

﴿Indeed you were a defiantly disobedient people,﴾ hypocrites. ﴿Nothing prevented their contributions from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾ — the first ﴿that﴾ is in the accusative position, and the second ﴿that﴾ is in the nominative position, its sense being: nothing prevented the acceptance of their contributions except their disbelief. ﴿And they do not come to prayer except while they are lazy,﴾ reluctant, because they do not hope for reward in performing it, nor do they fear punishment for abandoning it. ﴿And they do not spend except while they are unwilling,﴾ because they regard it as a burden and withholding it as a gain.

﴿So let not their wealth nor their children impress you,﴾ because when a servant is in Allah's Exalted gradual punishment [.........] [[Illegible text in the manuscript.]] ﴿Allah only intends to punish them thereby in the life of this world.﴾ Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi said: there is inversion and reordering in the verse; its sense: ﴿So let not their wealth nor their children impress you in the life of this world; Allah intends to punish them thereby in the Hereafter.﴾

Al-Hasan said: Allah only intends to punish them in the life of this world through zakat and spending in the cause of Allah. Ibn Zayd said: through the calamities in it. It was said: through the toil in gathering it, and the anxiety in guarding and loving it. ﴿And that their souls should depart﴾, that is, go forth, their souls perishing upon disbelief. It is said: "The horses zahaqat," meaning they went out of the racing course; "the arrow zahaqa" when it went out of the target; "falsehood zahaqa," meaning it vanished. ﴿Indeed you were a defiantly disobedient people,﴾ hypocrites. ﴿Nothing prevented their contributions from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾ — the first ﴿that﴾ is in the accusative position, and the second ﴿that﴾ is in the nominative position, its sense being: nothing prevented the acceptance of their contributions except their disbelief. ﴿And they do not come to prayer except while they are lazy,﴾ reluctant, because they do not hope for reward in performing it, nor do they fear punishment for abandoning it. ﴿And they do not spend except while they are unwilling,﴾ because they regard it as a burden and withholding it as a gain.

﴿So let not their wealth nor their children impress you,﴾ because when a servant is in Allah's Exalted gradual punishment [.........] [[Illegible text in the manuscript.]] ﴿Allah only intends to punish them thereby in the life of this world.﴾ Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi said: there is inversion and reordering in the verse; its sense: ﴿So let not their wealth nor their children impress you in the life of this world; Allah intends to punish them thereby in the Hereafter.﴾

Al-Hasan said: Allah only intends to punish them in the life of this world through zakat and spending in the cause of Allah. Ibn Zayd said: through the calamities in it. It was said: through the toil in gathering it, and the anxiety in guarding and loving it. ﴿And that their souls should depart﴾, that is, go forth, their souls perishing upon disbelief. It is said: "The horses zahaqat," meaning they went out of the racing course; "the arrow zahaqa" when it went out of the target; "falsehood zahaqa," meaning it vanished. Al-Mubarrad said: it has two forms: zahaqa yazhaqu and zahiqa yazhaqu.

﴿And they swear by Allah that they are surely of you,﴾ on your religion; ﴿but they are not of you, rather they are a people who are fearful (yafraqun)﴾, they fear. ﴿Were they to find a refuge (malja'an),﴾ meaning a shelter, a fortress and a stronghold; Ata said: a place of escape; Ibn Kaysan said: a people in whom they feel secure. ﴿Or caves (maghaarat),﴾ hollows in the mountains. Ata said: cellars. al-Akhfash said: everything you enter and vanish into is a maghara; it is a maf'ala form from "ghara al-rajul fi al-shay' yaghuru," when a man enters into something; from it comes "ghar al-ma'" (water sinking) and "ghârat al-'ayn" (the eye sinking into its socket), and from it "Ghawr Tihama," and al-ghawr is what is lowered of the land. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf recited maghaarat with a dammed mim, taking it as maf'al from "aghar yughir" when he hastens, and its meaning is a place of flight. The poet said:

So he counted its pursuers, and was counted away from them,
by a letter that has changed when he marched.

﴿Or a place of entry (mudkhalan)﴾, a place of entering. It is a mufta'al form from "tadakhkhala yatadakhkhalu, mutadakhkhil." Mujahid said: mudkhalan: a place of safety. Qatada: a tunnel. Al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd said: a burrow like that of the jerboa. al-Dahhak said: a refuge to which they retreat. al-Hasan said: a way in that they enter contrary to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Ibn Kaysan said: an entrance from which they cannot be reached by anything from you that they fear [from it]. al-Hasan recited: aw madkhalan, with the mim open and the dal light, from dakhala yadkhulu. Maslama ibn Muharib recited mudkhalan with the mim dammed and the dal lightened, from dakhala yadkhulu. Ubayy recited mundakhalan, a munfa'al form from indakhala, as the poet said:

So my hand is not in the hot cloth of the cloak [that] is pulled in.

Al-A'raj recited with a doubled dal and kha' [.........] [[Illegible text in the original.]], taking it as mutaf'al, then assimilating the ta' into the dal, as in al-muzzammil and al-muddaththir. ﴿They would turn away to it﴾, that is, they would retreat to it in flight from you. In the codex of Ubayy: "they would turn their faces to it." al-A'mash and al-'Uqayli recited: "lawaalu ilayhi" with an alif, from al-muwalah, meaning they would follow and hasten.

Mu'awiya ibn Nawfal narrated from his father, from his grandfather, who had been a Companion, that he recited: "lawallaw ilayhi" with a light lam, because it derives from al-tawliya, one says "wali ilayhi bi-nafsihi" when he turns toward it; and "wallaw ilayhi" from al-mawlin. ﴿While they rush headlong﴾, hastening in flight without anything turning them back. The poet Aban ibn Tha'laba said:

Swift and galloping, and its charging
like the blaze of a kindled palm frond.

It is said: jumuh is a movement between two gaits, and it is like al-sammah. Muhalhil said:

They rushed headlong in their blood,
until I saw the owners of their lineage fall dead.

al-A'mash recited: "wa-hum yajmizun," meaning they hasten and run. ﴿And among them﴾, meaning among the hypocrites, ﴿are those who find fault with you concerning the alms.﴾

al-Zuhri, from Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was dividing a distribution — Ibn 'Abbas said the spoils of Hawazin on the day of Hunayn — Ibn Dhi al-Khuwaysira al-Tamimi, who is Hurqus ibn Zuhayr, the root of the Kharijites, came and said: "Be just, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Woe to you! Who would be just if I am not just?"

'Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, permit me, and I will strike his neck." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Leave him, for he has companions, one of you belittles his prayer beside their prayer and his fasting beside their fasting. They pass out of the religion as an arrow passes through the game, one looks at its feathers and finds nothing on them, then looks at its shaft and finds nothing, and the dung and blood have passed. Their sign is a black man with one arm, or he said: one of his breasts, like a woman's breast or like a piece of flesh that shakes. They will come out at a time of division among the people." In another narration: "When they come out, kill them; then when they come out, kill them; then when they come out, kill them."

Then it was revealed: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the alms﴾, that is, they disparage you concerning its matter and attack you over it. It is said: "humazah lumazah." The poet said:

When I meet you from afar, you smile at me,
and when I am absent, you are the one who speaks ill and finds fault.

Mujahid said: yahmizuka: strikes at you. Ata said: yaghtabuka: backbites you. al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Raja', Salam and Ya'qub recited: yulmizuka with a dammed mim. Awf ibn Kathir narrated: yalmizka with a light kasra on the mim. ﴿If they are given from it, they are pleased; but if they are not given from it, behold, they become indignant.﴾ Ibn Zayd said: these hypocrites said: "By Allah, Muhammad will only give it to those he loves, and will only prefer those who are of his own inclination."

﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them﴾ (to) ﴿desirous (raghibun)﴾ — desiring that He would widen for us from His bounty, enriching us so that we need no alms or other people's wealth. Ibn 'Abbas said: desirous toward Him for what He gives us of reward, and averts from us of punishment.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 9, verse 50–59:

﴿If good befalls you, it grieves them,﴾ [meaning] the hypocrites; ﴿and if a calamity strikes you, they say, "We had already taken our precaution," meaning, we had made our excuse and resolved to sit back and abandon the raid, ﴿before this [calamity]﴾, before this misfortune.

﴿Say, "Nothing will befall us except what Allah has decreed for us,"﴾ say to them, O Muhammad. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "Say, 'Will anything befall us?'" and Talha ibn Musarrif recited it this way. ﴿except what Allah has written for us in the Preserved Tablet, and then decreed upon us. He is our Protector (mawla), our Guardian, our Helper and our Keeper.﴾ Al-Kalbi said: He is more deserving of us than ourselves, in death and in life. ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ ﴿Say, "Do you await for us anything but one of the two best outcomes?"﴾ Those being victory and conquest together with a great reward, or death as a martyr, in which is the great triumph.

Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi informed us, saying: Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Adl narrated to us; Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-'Abdi narrated to us; Abu Bakr Umayya ibn Bistam narrated to us; Yazid ibn Bazi' informed us, from Bakr ibn al-Qasim, from Suhayl, from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah guarantees to whoever goes out in His cause, with no motive for going out except belief in Allah and confirmation of His Messenger, that He will grant him martyrdom, or return him to his family forgiven, with whatever reward and spoils he has gained."

﴿And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Himself,﴾ so that Allah destroys them as He destroyed the earlier nations. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning thunderbolts. Ibn Jurayj said: meaning death, or punishment by slaying at our hands, as it befell the nations before us. ﴿So await,﴾ their destruction, ﴿indeed we are waiting along with you.﴾ Al-Hasan said: ﴿So await﴾ means the promises of Satan; ﴿indeed we are waiting along with you﴾ means the promises of Allah concerning the manifestation of His religion and the uprooting of those who oppose it. Satan used to hold out to them the hope of the death of the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿Say, "Spend willingly or unwillingly; it will never be accepted from you."﴾ It was revealed concerning Jadd ibn Qays when he asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to stay behind from the campaign, saying: "This is my wealth, I will help you with it." The apparent form of the verse is an imperative, but its meaning is a statement and a condition, its implied sense being: if you spend willingly or unwillingly, it will not be accepted from you, like the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them﴾ (the verse). When I meet you from afar, you smile at me,
and when I am absent, you are the one who speaks ill and finds fault.

Then he explained [to whom] the alms (ṣadaqāt) are given, saying, Mighty and Majestic is He who said: ﴿The alms are only for the poor and the needy﴾, not for the hypocrites. The scholars differed concerning the description of the poor (faqīr) and the needy (miskīn).

Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Jābir ibn Zayd, al-Zuhrī, Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: the faqīr is the one who refrains from asking, and the miskīn is the needy one who asks. Qatādah said: the faqīr is the believer who is in need [who has an affliction], and the miskīn is [the one who has no affliction].[[Addition from Zād al-Masīr: 3/309.]] Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī said: the poor (fuqarāʾ) are the poor among the Emigrants (muhājirūn), and the needy (masākīn) are the needy Muslims who did not emigrate. Ibn Salamah narrated from Ibn ʿUlayyah, from Ibn Sīrīn, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The faqīr is not the one who has no wealth, but the faqīr is the one whose earnings are worn out (al-akhlaq al-kasb)." Ibn ʿUlayyah said: "al-akhlaq here means al-muḥārif (the one whose livelihood has collapsed) according to us."[[Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī: 10/204.]] ʿIkrimah said: the poor (fuqarāʾ) are the poor Muslims, and the needy (masākīn) are from the People of the Book.

Abū Bakr al-ʿAbsī said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb saw a dhimmī, blind and cast down at the gate of the city, and ʿUmar said to him: "What is your condition?" He said: "They made me work on this island until my sight failed, and then they abandoned me; there is no one left who will give me anything." He said: "You have not been treated justly, then." So he ordered that he be given his sustenance and what would suffice him. Then he said: "This is among those whom Allah the Exalted meant when He said: ﴿The alms are only for the poor﴾, and they are the disabled among the People of the Book."[[Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 8/174; al-Muṣannaf of Ibn Abī Shaybah: 3/68.]] Ibn ʿAbbās said: the masākīn are [the wanderers] and the fuqarāʾ are from among the Muslims.[[Fatḥ al-Qadīr: 2/374.]]

We were informed by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥāmid: Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar informed us: Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd al-Muʾaddib narrated to us: ʿAbd al-Razzāq narrated to us, Maʿmar informed us, from Hammām ibn Munabbih, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The miskīn is not this wanderer who goes around among people, whom a morsel or two morsels and a date or two dates turn away. Rather, the miskīn is the one who does not find sufficiency to make him independent, and does not ask people, and is not noticed so that alms are given to him."[[Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr: 1/214.]]

Al-Farrāʾ said: the fuqarāʾ are the People of the Ṣuffah, who had no clans and no wealth; they would seek provision and then take shelter in the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The masākīn are those who wander around the doors.[[Tāj al-ʿArūs: 3/473.]] ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan said: the miskīn is the one who is humble and submissive even if he does not ask, and the faqīr is the one who bears [hardship] and accepts something discreetly and is not humble. [Ibn al-Sikkīt, al-Qutaybī and Yūnus] said: the faqīr is the one who has the bare subsistence of life, and the miskīn is the one who has nothing at all. He cited the verse of the poet:

Indeed the faqīr is the one whose milch-camel
was just enough for his dependants, and left him no surplus (sabad).[[al-Ṣiḥāḥ: 2/782.]]

Here he gave him a milch-camel, and made it a provision for his dependants, meaning sustenance with no surplus in it. What confirms this is what is narrated from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abzā, who said: "Some of the Emigrants had a house, a wife, a slave, and a she-camel on which he performed Ḥajj and went to war, and Allah the Exalted attributed to them the description of poverty and assigned them a share in zakāh."[[Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī: 10/204.]]

Muḥammad ibn Maslamah said: the faqīr is the one who has a dwelling in which he lives, and a servant, up to [.......] [[Illegible words in the manuscript.]] because that is the miskīn who has no possession. They said: everyone who is in need of something is dependent upon it, even if he is wealthy in other respects. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor toward Allah﴾, and the miskīn is one who is in need of everything. Do you not see how He urged feeding him, and made the expiation (kaffārah) consist of food for him? And there is no greater poverty than [.....] [[Illegible words in the manuscript.]] in the severity of hunger.

As for His saying: ﴿As for the ship, it belonged to the masākīn﴾, their being called masākīn here is in the sense of compassion and self-restraint, not because they owned the ship, just as one who is afflicted with a calamity or is subjected to a trial is called "miskīn."

In a ḥadīth: "the miskīn of the people of the Fire." And a poet said:

The lovers' miskīn ones, until their graves,
upon them is the dust of humiliation among the tombs.[[Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 8/170.]]

﴿And those who work upon it﴾: meaning its collectors and receivers, who undertake to take it from its people and place it in its rightful place, and who labor for it; they are given that as payment, whether they are rich or poor.

They differed concerning the amount they are given. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: they are given one-eighth of the alms. Mujāhid said: the workers eat from the eighth share. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ said: they are given according to the extent of their labor; this is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Yaʿfūr, who said: they are given according to the wages of their equals, even if it exceeds one-eighth. What confirms this is the statement of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd, who said: "ʿUmar and those men did not give the worker an eighth; rather, they set for him an amount according to his work."[[Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī: 10/207.]] Mālik and the people of Iraq said: this is left to the Imam and his discretion; the Imam gives them according to what he sees fit.

﴿And those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾: Qatādah said: they are some people from the Bedouins and others whom the Prophet (ﷺ) would win over with gifts so that they might believe. Maʿqil ibn ʿAbd Allāh said: I asked al-Zuhrī about "those whose hearts are to be reconciled," and he said: "Whoever among Jews or Christians has embraced Islam." I said: "Even if he is wealthy?" He said: "Even if he is wealthy."

Ibn ʿAbbās said: they are people who had embraced Islam, who would come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and he would give them a small portion from the alms; when he gave them from the alms and they gained some good from it, they would say: "This is a good religion." But if it was otherwise, they would find fault with it and abandon it.

Ibn Kaysān said: they are people from among the people of war whom the Prophet (ﷺ) would win over with alms so that they would refrain from fighting him.

al-Kalbī, Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr and others said: they are the men of distinction among the tribes, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would give in Islam to win them over, and they are those among whom he divided camels on the day of Ḥunayn. They were: from Banū Makhzūm, al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yarbūʿ; from Banū Umayyah, Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb; and from Banū Jumaḥ, Ṣafwān ibn Umayyah; from Banū ʿĀmir ibn Lu'ayy, Suhayl ibn ʿAmr and Ḥuwayṭib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā; from Banū Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, Ḥakīm ibn Khizām; from Banū Hāshim, Abū Sufyān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; from Banū Fazārah, ʿUyaynah ibn Ḥiṣn and Ḥudhayfah ibn Badr; from Banū Tamīm, al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis; from Banū al-Naḍr, Mālik ibn ʿAwf ibn Mālik; from Banū Sulaym, al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās; from Banū Thaqīf, al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Khārijah. The Prophet (ﷺ) gave each man of them one hundred camels, except ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yarbūʿ and Ḥuwayṭib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā. He said: in another narration: Makhramah ibn Nawfal, ʿUmayr ibn Wahb and Hishām ibn ʿAmr.

al-Kalbī added: Abū al-Baʿāʾil ibn Yaʿkul, Judd ibn Qays al-Sahmī, ʿAmr ibn Mirdās and Hishām ibn ʿAmr. He said: he gave each one of them fifty camels.[[Naṣb al-Rāyah: 2/476.]] Al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās said about that to the Prophet (ﷺ):

So my share and the share of the slaves became
between ʿUyaynah and al-Aqraʿ.
Ḥiṣn and Ḥābis did not
surpass Mirdās in the assembly.
Though I was in war one of strength,
I was given nothing and I was not withheld from.
Except for a few of the camels I was given,
their number being of four legs,
And raids which I averted
with my brave charge on the mare in the open plain,
And my waking of the people, when they slept
while the people slept and I did not sleep,
And I was not below either of the two men,
and whoever is lowered today will not be raised.[[Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 8/180, with some transposition.]]

So the Prophet (ﷺ) gave him one hundred camels. He gave Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām seventy camels, and he said: "O Messenger of Allah, I did not know that anyone had a better claim to your gift than I do." So he added ten young camels to him, then added ten more young camels until he completed one hundred for him. Ḥakīm said: "O Messenger of Allah, is the gift you gave me which I disliked better, or this which you increased?" He said: "No, rather this which you desired." He said: "I will not take other than it," so he took the seventy. Ḥakīm died while he was the wealthiest man of Quraysh.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I give to one man and leave another, and the one I leave is dearer to me than the one I give to. But I win this one over with the gift, and I entrust the believer to his faith." [22]

Ṣafwān ibn Umayyah said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave me what he gave me, and he was the most hated of people to me, yet he did not cease giving me until he became the most beloved of people to me."

Then they differed concerning the existence of "those whose hearts are to be reconciled" today, and whether they are given from the alms and other than it or not. Al-Ḥasan said: "As for those whose hearts are to be reconciled, they do not exist today." Al-Shaʿbī said: "There remain none of those whose hearts are to be reconciled among the people today; they existed only in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When Abū Bakr came to power, the bribes ceased." This is the interpretation of the people of the Qur'an. It is supported by the ḥadīth of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb when ʿUyaynah ibn Ḥiṣn came to him and [he] said: ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills let him believe, and whoever wills let him disbelieve﴾; "Islam is too exalted to be bought with bribes," meaning there are no reconciled ones today.

Abū ʿAwānah narrated from Muhājir Abū al-Ḥasan, who said: "I came to Abū Wāʾil and Abū Burdah with zakāh, and they were in charge of the treasury, so they took it. Then I came again and found Abū Wāʾil alone, and he said: 'Return it and place it in its proper places.' I said: 'Then what should I do with the share of those whose hearts are to be reconciled?' He said: 'Return it to the others.'"

Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī said: "Among people today, those whose hearts are to be reconciled are established," and this is the view of Abū Thawr, who said: "They have a share which the Imam gives them according to what he sees."

al-Shāfiʿī said: "Those whose hearts are to be reconciled are of two kinds: one kind is polytheists, who are not given; and another kind is Muslims [who, if the Imam gives them, restrain their evil from the Muslims]. I am of the view that they be given from the share of the Prophet, which is one-fifth of the fifth, what they are reconciled with, in addition to their share with the Muslims. What supports this is that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave to those whose hearts are to be reconciled after Allah had opened conquests for him, Islam had spread, and its people had been strengthened. As for their share of zakāh, I am of the view that it be spent on strengthening the religion and filling the needs of Islam, and that no polytheist who is reconciled to Islam be given; for Allah the Exalted is certainly able to make His religion independent of that. And Allah knows best."

﴿And for the captives (fī al-riqāb)﴾ — abridged; meaning for freeing necks from bondage. The scholars differed about them. Most jurists said they are the mukātabūn (slaves contracted to purchase their freedom). This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and al-Layth ibn Saʿd. It is narrated that a mukātab stood before Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī while he was addressing the people on Friday and said: "O Amir, urge the people on my behalf." So Abū Mūsā urged them, and the people threw cloaks, turbans and rings until a great quantity of goods was thrown upon him. When Abū Mūsā saw what the people had thrown, he said: "Gather it." It was gathered, then he ordered it sold, and he gave the mukātab his contracted sum, then gave the surplus to the captives and did not return it to the people, and said: "I only gave to the people for the captives."[[Naṣb al-Rāyah: 2/477.]]

al-Ḥasan and Ibn ʿAbbās said: slaves are freed from it; this is the position of Mālik, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Thawr. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Nakhaʿī said: a whole slave is not freed from zakāh, but it is given at a designated time for the freeing of a mukātab; this is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah, Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad.

al-Zuhrī said: the share of the captives is in two halves: half for every mukātab who professes Islam, and the second half for purchasing slaves who have prayed and fasted and whose Islam is established, male or female, to be freed for Allah.[[al-Durr al-Manthūr: 3/252.]]

﴿And the debtors (al-gharimīn)﴾: Qatādah said: they are people whom debts have overwhelmed, not from extravagance, nor wastefulness, nor corruption.[[Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī: 10/211.]] Mujāhid said: one whose house has burned down, or whose wealth has been swept away by a flood, and who has incurred debt for his dependants.[[Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī: 10/211.]]

Abū Jaʿfar al-Bāqir said: the debtors are of two kinds: one kind who borrowed for their own benefit, or for some good, or for something not sinful, then were unable to pay it from goods or cash, so they are given for their debt; and another kind who borrowed for reconciliation between people, good works, and mutual settlement, and who have goods which, if sold, would harm them, so these are given the value of their goods.[[See Kitāb al-Umm of al-Shāfiʿī: 2/78.]]

This applies when their debt was not for disobedience, nor extravagance, nor sin. As for one who borrowed for the disobedience of Allah, I do not think he should be given. The root of gharam is loss and deficiency; from it comes the ḥadīth: "For the one who is protected, his gain, and upon him his loss (gharam)." From this also the punishment is called gharām; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed its punishment was ever gharāman (lasting destruction)﴾. And so-and-so is "mughram" with women, meaning destroyed by them; how severe is his infatuation (gharām) and his being smitten (ighrām) with women.

﴿And in the way of Allah﴾: among them are the warriors, the garrison-holders (al-murābiṭūn), and the needy.

As for when they are wealthy, they differed about it. Abū Ḥanīfah, Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad said: the warrior is not given unless he is cut off and destitute. Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Isḥāq, Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Thawr said: the warrior is given from it even if he is wealthy. What supports this is the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Charity is not lawful for a wealthy person except for five: a man who works for it, or a man who buys it with his wealth, or one in the way of Allah, or the wayfarer (ibn al-sabīl), or a man who had a neighbor who gave him charity and he gave it to him as a gift."[23][[Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī: 10/212.]]

﴿And the wayfarer (ibn al-sabīl)﴾: the traveler who passes through; he was named "son of the road" because of his constant attachment to it, like the poet's saying:

O son of war, return me as a child
until I grow up and my contemporaries are complete.

Mujāhid and al-Zuhrī said: the wayfarer has a right to zakāh even if he is wealthy, if he is in need of it. Mālik and the jurists of Iraq said: he is the cut-off pilgrim. al-Shāfiʿī said: the wayfarer is among the [neighbors] of charity who wish to travel for something not sinful, and are unable to reach their destination except with assistance. Qatādah said: he is the guest.

﴿An obligation﴾ from Allah: it is in the accusative of emphasis according to al-Kisāʾī, and in the accusative of the infinitive according to Sībawayh, meaning Allah has made these things an obligation. Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAblah said: he read farīḍatun in the nominative, making it a predicate, as you say: "innamā yazīdu khārij." ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾.

The scholars differed about how the alms mentioned in this verse are to be divided: whether each of these eight categories has a right in it, or whether that is left to the owner of the wealth and to whoever is in charge of distributing it, so that he may give all of it to whichever of the eight categories he wills. Some said: he has the right to divide it and place it among whichever categories he wills, and Allah the Exalted only named the eight categories in the verse to inform that the alms do not go outside these categories to others, not to require an equal division among them. This is the view of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, Ḥudhayfah, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn [Jubayr], ʿAṭāʾ, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Maymūn ibn Mihrān and Abū Ḥanīfah.

We were informed by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥāmid: Abū Bakr al-Ṭabarī informed us: ʿAlī ibn Ḥarb narrated to us, Ibn Fuḍayl informed us, ʿAṭāʾ narrated to us, from Saʿīd concerning ﴿The alms are only for the poor﴾ the verse: whichever of these categories you find, it suffices for you to give your alms to him. Abū Ḥanīfah said: it is permissible to limit it to one poor person. Mālik said: it is given to the one most in need of it.

al-Shāfiʿī used to apply the verse to its apparent meaning, and said: if the owner of the wealth undertakes its distribution, he must place it among three categories, because the share of those whose hearts are reconciled has lapsed, and the share of the workers is nullified by his own distribution of it. If the Imam undertakes its distribution, he must divide it among seven categories, and it suffices him to give from each category fewer than three persons, and no one may divert the share or any part of it from its people who deserve it; and he may not take it out of a land in which there is someone entitled to it to give it to those who are found from among the categories. This is the view of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, ʿIkrimah and al-Zuhrī.

Then he returned to mention the hypocrites and said: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, "He is an ear"﴾ — meaning among the hypocrites. It was revealed concerning Ḥizām ibn Khālid, al-Jullās ibn Suwayd, Iyās ibn Qays, Makhshī ibn Khuwaylid, Simāk ibn Yazīd, ʿUbayd ibn Hilāl, Rifāʿah ibn al-Miqdād, ʿUbaydah ibn Mālik and Rifāʿah ibn Zayd, who used to harm the Prophet (ﷺ) and say what was not fitting. Some of them said: "Do not do what they say, lest it befall us." Al-Jullās said: "Rather, we will say whatever we wish, then we will go to him and he will confirm to us what we say, for Muḥammad is merely an ear that listens." So Allah revealed this verse.[[Zād al-Masīr: 3/312.]]

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq said, from Yasār and others: it was revealed concerning a man among the hypocrites called Nahshal ibn al-Ḥārith, who was bareheaded, red-eyed, with sunken cheeks and deformed appearance, and he is the one about whom the Prophet (ﷺ) said:

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 9, verses 60–69 (part 2 of 2)**
