They built the Mosque of Harm so that some of them would pray in it instead of the Mosque of Quba, and some would pray in the Mosque of Quba, so they would disagree and divide because of it. ﴿And in preparation﴾: waiting and readying for ﴿those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger﴾ earlier, namely Abu Amir the monk, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called "the Fasiq," so that he would pray in it when he returned from Syria, and prevail over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Al-A'mash recited: ﴿wa-irsadan lil-ladhina harabu Allah﴾ (for those who warred against Allah). ﴿And they will swear, "We intended only the good"﴾: they intended only the good deed, which was for the sick among the Muslims, the extension of relief for the weak and the ill, and those unable to travel to the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿And Allah testifies that they are liars﴾ in their words and oaths. Then He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Do not stand in it ever﴾.

﴿Indeed, a mosque founded on piety﴾: the lam here is the lam of initiation and oath, meaning "By Allah, indeed a mosque..." ﴿was founded on piety﴾: its foundation was laid and its construction began. ﴿From the first day﴾: from the first day it was built. It was said that the meaning is: since the first day its foundation was laid. Al-Mubarrad said: It was said concerning the meaning of the phrase "min hajj wa-amn dahr" (from pilgrimage and security through time), i.e., "the one who is pilgrimage and security throughout time." Zuhayr composed:

"To whom belong the abodes at the Qunnat al-Hijr,
which have become desolate from pilgrimage and from time?"

[[Al-Sihah by al-Jawhari: 6/2209; Lisan al-Arab: 4/170, citing only the first half.]]

Meaning: since the pilgrimage and since time. ﴿More worthy﴾: more deserving that you ﴿stand in it﴾ in prayer. The scholars differed concerning which mosque is ﴿founded on piety﴾. Some said it is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in which are his pulpit and his grave.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us, and al-Abdi informed us: Ahmad ibn Najdah narrated to us, al-Jamani narrated to us, Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from Uthman ibn Abdullah ibn Abi Rafi', from Ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The mosque founded on piety is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is indicated by what was narrated:

Humayd al-Kharrat narrated from Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, that Abd al-Rahman told him that he entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the house of one of his wives. He said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, which mosque is founded on piety?" He took a handful of pebbles and struck them on the ground, then said: "It is your mosque here, the Mosque of Madinah."

Anas ibn Abi Yahya narrated from his father, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: it is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Awfi said: it is the Mosque of Quba. They both came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this, and he said: "It is this one," meaning the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Ibn Yazid, Ibn Zayd, and Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: it is the Mosque of Quba. This is also the narration of Ali ibn Abi Talhah and Atiyyah from Ibn Abbas.

﴿In it are men who love that they purify themselves﴾: from ritual impurities and filth with water. Al-Kalbi said: it is washing the rear with water. Ata' said: they used to cleanse themselves with water and would not sleep at night in a state of major impurity.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the people of Quba when this verse was revealed: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has praised you concerning purification. What is it?" They said: "We cleanse ourselves with water" [[Kanz al-Ummal: 13/7, hadith 33709.]].

﴿And Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾: i.e., those who are purified. The taa' was assimilated into the taa' (ta') because their points of articulation are close.

Yazid ibn Ajrah said: Fever came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the form of a black slave-girl. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her, "Who are you?" She said: "Umm MalDam; I drink blood, eat flesh, yellow the face, and thin the bone."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Then go to the Ansar, for they have rights over us." So fever struck the Ansar.

The next day he said: "What is the matter with the Ansar?" It was said: "They have all been stricken with fever." He said: "Come, let us go and visit them." He visited them and kept saying: "Rejoice, for it is an expiation and a purification" [59].

They said: "O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that it may remain with us for years, so that it may be an expiation for our sins." Then Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾ through fever from their sins, ﴿and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾ from sins.

﴿Is one who founded his building﴾: The readers differed about it. Nafi' and the people of Syria recited ﴿Assisa bunyanuhu﴾ with a damma on the hamza and the nun, in the passive form. Abu Hatim mentioned it from Zayd ibn Thabit. Imarah ibn Sa'id recited ﴿Ā'assa﴾ with a long vowel, a fatha on the sin and the nun, in the pattern of "amana." Likewise the second instance. ﴿Ā'assa, assa, and assasa﴾ have the same meaning; af'ala and fa''ala are close in transitivity.

The rest recited with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the first sin, in the active form, and Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this.

﴿Upon piety from Allah﴾. Isa ibn Umar recited ﴿taqwan min Allah﴾ with tanwin. ﴿And approval is better, or one who founded his building upon the brink﴾: i.e., the edge. Abu Ubayd said: al-shafa is the border, and its dual is al-shafawan.

﴿Of a crumbling cliff﴾: Asim and Hamzah recited it with a light pronunciation, and the rest with a heavy pronunciation; both are dialects. It refers to a well that has not been trodden. Abu Ubaydah said: it is a pit, and what the torrent washes out of the valleys. ﴿Crumbling﴾ (hari): i.e., falling, the one that collapses piece by piece as sand or soft material crumbles. It is said it is an inverted form: its yā' is moved and postponed, so it is said "hār," as one says "shākī al-silāḥ" and "shā'ik al-silāḥ," and "āq" and "ā'iq." The poet said:

"And an obstacle did not prevent me from her love."

It was also said: it is from hāra yahāru, meaning it collapsed, like khāfa yakhāfu. This is an example of the weakness of their intentions and the scarcity of their insight in knowledge. ﴿And it collapsed﴾: it was scattered. It is said: hāra and inhāra and yahūru have the same meaning, meaning it fell and was demolished. From this it is said "tahawwara al-layl" (the night passed) when most of it has gone. In the codex of Ubayy: "and its foundations collapsed with it." ﴿Into the fire of Hell. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

Qatadah said: By Allah, [it did not wait long] before it fell into the Fire. It was mentioned to us that a pit was dug in that place, and they saw smoke coming out of it. Jabir ibn Abdullah said: I saw smoke coming out of the Mosque of Harm. Khalaf ibn Yasin al-Kufi said: I performed Hajj with my father in the time of the Umayyads, and I saw in Madinah the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs, meaning the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Quba, in which is the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis. When the time of Abu Ja'far came, they said: "The ignorant person enters and does not recognize the qiblah." So the building that had been built at the hands of Abd al-Samad ibn Ali was demolished. And I saw the mosque of the hypocrites that Allah, Exalted, mentioned in the Qur'an, and in it was a hole from which smoke comes out, and today it is a rubbish heap [[Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/405.]].

﴿Their building which they built will not cease to be a doubt﴾ in their hearts: doubt and hypocrisy. ﴿In their hearts﴾. They think that by building it they were doing good, just as the calf was made beloved to the people of Musa. Ibn Abbas said: doubt and hypocrisy. Al-Kalbi said: he made it beloved and adorned it, because they claimed they would not follow him. Al-Suddi, Habib, and al-Mubarrad said: because Allah demolished their building, which they built, leaving a rancor in their hearts. ﴿Unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾: their hearts are torn apart so that they die, like His words: ﴿We would have severed from him the aorta﴾ [[Surah al-Haqqah 69:46.]], because life ends when the heart is severed.

Al-Hasan, Ya'qub, and Abu Hatim recited: ﴿ilā an tuqatta'a﴾ with a light pronunciation, meaning "until," as a limit. The interpretation of al-Dahhak and Qatadah supports this: they will remain in doubt until they die, and then they will be certain and will know clearly.

The readers differed about His words ﴿taqatta'a﴾. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Ibn Amir, Hamzah, al-Mufaddal, and Hafs recited ﴿taqatta'a﴾ with a fatha on the taa' and the ta', with a shadda, meaning "taqatta'a," then one of the two taa's was deleted. Yahya ibn Kathir, Mujahid, Nafi', Asim, Abu Amr, and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿tuqatti'a﴾ with a damma on the taa' and a shadda on the ta', in the passive form, and this is the choice of Abu Ubaydah and Abu Hatim. Ya'qub recited ﴿tuqta'a﴾ with a damma on the taa' and a light pronunciation, from the root "qata'a" (to cut).

It is narrated from Ibn Kathir "taqta'a" with a fatha on the taa' and a light pronunciation. ﴿Qulubahum﴾ (their hearts) is in the accusative, meaning that you yourself do that to them. Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash recited: ﴿wa-law qutti'at qulubuhum﴾ (even if their hearts were cut).

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

And others are deferred until Allah's command: that is, delayed, so that He may decide concerning them what He decides.

They are the three who stayed behind and tied themselves to the pillars, and who did not go to great lengths in repentance and apology as Abu Lubabah and his companions did. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was gentle with them, forbade people from speaking to them, and ordered their wives to separate from them, until anxiety overwhelmed them and grief tore them apart. The earth became constricted for them despite its vastness. They had been among the people of Badr, so people began saying, "They are ruined, unless an excuse is revealed for them." Others began saying, "Perhaps Allah will forgive them." They were left waiting for Allah's command, not knowing whether they would be punished or shown mercy, until Allah accepted their repentance after fifty nights and revealed ﴿And [He also turned in forgiveness] to the three who were left behind﴾.

Allah's words: ﴿And those who took a mosque for harm﴾, the verse.

The exegetes said: The Banu Amr ibn Awf built the Mosque of Quba and sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), asking him to come and pray in it. He came and prayed in it. Their brothers, the Banu Ghanm ibn Awf, envied them and said, "We will build a mosque and send to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to pray in it, as he prayed in our brothers' mosque, and Abu Amir al-Nu'man the monk will pray in it when he returns from Syria." Abu Amir was a man from among them; he was the father of Hanzalah, "the one washed by the angels." He had become a monk in the Jahiliyyah, had embraced Christianity, and had worn coarse wool. When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah, Abu Amir said to him, "What is this that you have brought?" He said, "I have brought the Hanifiyyah, the religion of Ibrahim." Abu Amir said, "I am upon it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "You are not upon it." He said, "Yes, but you have introduced into the Hanifiyyah what is not part of it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "I have not done that; rather, I have brought it pure and white." Then he said to the Prophet (ﷺ):

"May Allah cause the liar among us to die, a lone exile."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Amin." He was named "the Fasiq" (the transgressor). When the day of Uhud came, Abu Amir said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "If I find a people who fight you, I will fight you alongside them." He continued fighting him until the day of Hunayn. When Hawazin was defeated, he went out to the Romans seeking support, and he sent to the hypocrites: "Prepare whatever strength and weapons you can, and build me a mosque, for I am going to Caesar, the king of the Romans, to bring an army of Romans to expel Muhammad and his companions." This is Allah's words: ﴿and in preparation for those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger﴾.

So they built a mosque beside the Mosque of Quba. Those who built it were twelve men: Khidham ibn Khalid, from whose house the mosque was taken; Tha'labah ibn Hatib; Mu'tib ibn Qushayr; Abu al-Ara'd; Abbad ibn Hunayf; Harithah ibn Amir; [Jariyah and his two sons] [[The correction is from Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi: 175.]] Mujammi' and Zayd; Nabtal ibn al-Harith; Lahhad ibn Uthman; and Wadi'ah ibn Thabit. Mujammi' ibn Yazid led them in prayer. When they finished, they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was preparing for Tabuk, and said, "O Messenger of Allah, we have built a mosque for the sick, for those in need, for rainy nights and cold nights. We would love for you to come to us, pray in it for us, and invoke blessing." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "I am about to set out on a journey. If we return, Allah willing, we will come to you and pray for you there" [57].

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from Tabuk and stopped at Dhu Awan, a place an hour's distance from Madinah, they asked him to come to their mosque. He called for his garment to wear, intending to go to them, but the Qur'an was revealed to him, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed him about the Mosque of Harm and what they had planned. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned Malik ibn al-Dukhshum, Ma'n ibn Adi, Amir ibn al-Sakan, and al-Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah, and said to them, "Go to this wrongdoing mosque and its people; demolish it and burn it." They went out quickly until they reached Salim ibn Awf. They also came to the family of Malik ibn al-Dukhshum. Malik said to them, "Wait until I bring you fire from my family." He entered his household, took palm fronds, and lit them into fire. Then they went out chanting until they entered the mosque while its people were inside. They burned and demolished it, and its people scattered from it. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that it be made into a dunghill where carrion, filth, and refuse would be thrown. Abu Amir the monk died in Syria, alone and a stranger. About it Ka'b ibn Malik said:

"Allah forbid, from the deed of the wicked,
like your effort among the clan, O Abd Amr.
As for your claim that you have nobility and palms,
you have sold faith for disbelief."

[[The full story is mentioned in Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, 175; Zad al-Masir: 3/339; and the poem in al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham: 2/424.]]

Ikrimah said: Umar ibn al-Khattab asked one of them, "What did you contribute to this mosque?" He said, "I contributed a pillar." Umar said, "Rejoice in it, around your neck in the Fire of Hell."

It is also narrated that the Banu Amr ibn Awf, who built the Mosque of Quba, asked Umar ibn al-Khattab during his caliphate to permit Mujammi' ibn Harithah to lead them in prayer in their mosque. He said, "No, and no blessing to the eye. Is it not the Mosque of Harm?" Mujammi' said to him, "O Commander of the Faithful, do not hasten against me. By Allah, I prayed in it, and I do not know what they concealed in it. I was a young man who recited the Qur'an, and they were a steadfast people who were eager, and they knew nothing of the Qur'an. So I prayed, and I do not think they were prevented from anything, except that they were humbling themselves before Allah. I did not know what was in their hearts."

Umar accepted his excuse, believed him, and ordered him to pray in the Mosque of Quba.

This is the story of the Mosque of Harm in which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed ﴿And those who took a mosque﴾. The common readers recited it with the wa (and), while the people of Madinah and Syria recited it without the wa. It is also so in the codices of the people of Madinah and Syria.

Ata' said: When Allah granted Umar ibn al-Khattab the conquest of the cities, he ordered the Muslims to build mosques and ordered them not to make two mosques in one city, one adjacent to the other.

Layth narrated that Shaqiq did not attend prayer in the mosque of Banu Amir. It was said to him, "The mosque of Banu so-and-so, they have not prayed in it yet." He said, "I do not like to pray in it, for it was built on harm. Every mosque built for harm, display, or reputation will ultimately trace back to the Mosque of Harm" [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/36.]].

﴿And disbelief﴾: hypocrisy. ﴿And division among the believers﴾: they divide their community with it, because they used to pray together in the Mosque of Quba. They built the Mosque of Harm so that some of them would pray in it instead of the Mosque of Quba, and some would pray in the Mosque of Quba, so they would disagree and divide because of it. ﴿And in preparation﴾: waiting and readying for ﴿those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger﴾ earlier, namely Abu Amir the monk, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called "the Fasiq," so that he would pray in it when he returned from Syria, and prevail over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Al-A'mash recited: ﴿wa-irsadan lil-ladhina harabu Allah﴾ (for those who warred against Allah). ﴿And they will swear, "We intended only the good"﴾: they intended only the good deed, which was for the sick among the Muslims, the extension of relief for the weak and the ill, and those unable to travel to the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿And Allah testifies that they are liars﴾ in their words and oaths. Then He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Do not stand in it ever﴾.

﴿Indeed, a mosque founded on piety﴾: the lam here is the lam of initiation and oath, meaning "By Allah, indeed a mosque..." ﴿was founded on piety﴾: its foundation was laid and its construction began. ﴿From the first day﴾: from the first day it was built. It was said that the meaning is: since the first day its foundation was laid. Al-Mubarrad said: It was said concerning the meaning of the phrase "min hajj wa-amn dahr" (from pilgrimage and security through time), i.e., "the one who is pilgrimage and security throughout time." Zuhayr composed:

"To whom belong the abodes at the Qunnat al-Hijr,
which have become desolate from pilgrimage and from time?"

[[Al-Sihah by al-Jawhari: 6/2209; Lisan al-Arab: 4/170, citing only the first half.]]

Meaning: since the pilgrimage and since time. ﴿More worthy﴾: more deserving that you ﴿stand in it﴾ in prayer. The scholars differed concerning which mosque is ﴿founded on piety﴾. Some said it is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in which are his pulpit and his grave.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us, and al-Abdi informed us: Ahmad ibn Najdah narrated to us, al-Jamani narrated to us, Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from Uthman ibn Abdullah ibn Abi Rafi', from Ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The mosque founded on piety is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is indicated by what was narrated:

Humayd al-Kharrat narrated from Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, that Abd al-Rahman told him that he entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the house of one of his wives. He said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, which mosque is founded on piety?" He took a handful of pebbles and struck them on the ground, then said: "It is your mosque here, the Mosque of Madinah."

Anas ibn Abi Yahya narrated from his father, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: it is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Awfi said: it is the Mosque of Quba. They both came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this, and he said: "It is this one," meaning the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Ibn Yazid, Ibn Zayd, and Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: it is the Mosque of Quba. This is also the narration of Ali ibn Abi Talhah and Atiyyah from Ibn Abbas.

﴿In it are men who love that they purify themselves﴾: from ritual impurities and filth with water. Al-Kalbi said: it is washing the rear with water. Ata' said: they used to cleanse themselves with water and would not sleep at night in a state of major impurity.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the people of Quba when this verse was revealed: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has praised you concerning purification. What is it?" They said: "We cleanse ourselves with water" [[Kanz al-Ummal: 13/7, hadith 33709.]].

﴿And Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾: i.e., those who are purified. The taa' was assimilated into the taa' (ta') because their points of articulation are close.

Yazid ibn Ajrah said: Fever came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the form of a black slave-girl. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her, "Who are you?" She said: "Umm MalDam; I drink blood, eat flesh, yellow the face, and thin the bone."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Then go to the Ansar, for they have rights over us." So fever struck the Ansar.

The next day he said: "What is the matter with the Ansar?" It was said: "They have all been stricken with fever." He said: "Come, let us go and visit them." He visited them and kept saying: "Rejoice, for it is an expiation and a purification" [59].

They said: "O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that it may remain with us for years, so that it may be an expiation for our sins." Then Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾ through fever from their sins, ﴿and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾ from sins.

﴿Is one who founded his building﴾: The readers differed about it. Nafi' and the people of Syria recited ﴿Assisa bunyanuhu﴾ with a damma on the hamza and the nun, in the passive form. Abu Hatim mentioned it from Zayd ibn Thabit. Imarah ibn Sa'id recited ﴿Ā'assa﴾ with a long vowel, a fatha on the sin and the nun, in the pattern of "amana." Likewise the second instance. ﴿Ā'assa, assa, and assasa﴾ have the same meaning; af'ala and fa''ala are close in transitivity.

The rest recited with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the first sin, in the active form, and Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this.

﴿Upon piety from Allah﴾. Isa ibn Umar recited ﴿taqwan min Allah﴾ with tanwin. ﴿And approval is better, or one who founded his building upon the brink﴾: i.e., the edge. Abu Ubayd said: al-shafa is the border, and its dual is al-shafawan.

﴿Of a crumbling cliff﴾: Asim and Hamzah recited it with a light pronunciation, and the rest with a heavy pronunciation; both are dialects. It refers to a well that has not been trodden. Abu Ubaydah said: it is a pit, and what the torrent washes out of the valleys. ﴿Crumbling﴾ (hari): i.e., falling, the one that collapses piece by piece as sand or soft material crumbles. It is said it is an inverted form: its yā' is moved and postponed, so it is said "hār," as one says "shākī al-silāḥ" and "shā'ik al-silāḥ," and "āq" and "ā'iq." The poet said:

"And an obstacle did not prevent me from her love."

It was also said: it is from hāra yahāru, meaning it collapsed, like khāfa yakhāfu. This is an example of the weakness of their intentions and the scarcity of their insight in knowledge. ﴿And it collapsed﴾: it was scattered. It is said: hāra and inhāra and yahūru have the same meaning, meaning it fell and was demolished. From this it is said "tahawwara al-layl" (the night passed) when most of it has gone. In the codex of Ubayy: "and its foundations collapsed with it." ﴿Into the fire of Hell. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

Qatadah said: By Allah, [it did not wait long] before it fell into the Fire. It was mentioned to us that a pit was dug in that place, and they saw smoke coming out of it. Jabir ibn Abdullah said: I saw smoke coming out of the Mosque of Harm. Khalaf ibn Yasin al-Kufi said: I performed Hajj with my father in the time of the Umayyads, and I saw in Madinah the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs, meaning the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Quba, in which is the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis. When the time of Abu Ja'far came, they said: "The ignorant person enters and does not recognize the qiblah." So the building that had been built at the hands of Abd al-Samad ibn Ali was demolished. And I saw the mosque of the hypocrites that Allah, Exalted, mentioned in the Qur'an, and in it was a hole from which smoke comes out, and today it is a rubbish heap [[Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/405.]].

﴿Their building which they built will not cease to be a doubt﴾ in their hearts: doubt and hypocrisy. ﴿In their hearts﴾. They think that by building it they were doing good, just as the calf was made beloved to the people of Musa. Ibn Abbas said: doubt and hypocrisy. Al-Kalbi said: he made it beloved and adorned it, because they claimed they would not follow him. Al-Suddi, Habib, and al-Mubarrad said: because Allah demolished their building, which they built, leaving a rancor in their hearts. ﴿Unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾: their hearts are torn apart so that they die, like His words: ﴿We would have severed from him the aorta﴾ [[Surah al-Haqqah 69:46.]], because life ends when the heart is severed.

Al-Hasan, Ya'qub, and Abu Hatim recited: ﴿ilā an tuqatta'a﴾ with a light pronunciation, meaning "until," as a limit. The interpretation of al-Dahhak and Qatadah supports this: they will remain in doubt until they die, and then they will be certain and will know clearly.

The readers differed about His words ﴿taqatta'a﴾. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Ibn Amir, Hamzah, al-Mufaddal, and Hafs recited ﴿taqatta'a﴾ with a fatha on the taa' and the ta', with a shadda, meaning "taqatta'a," then one of the two taa's was deleted. Yahya ibn Kathir, Mujahid, Nafi', Asim, Abu Amr, and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿tuqatti'a﴾ with a damma on the taa' and a shadda on the ta', in the passive form, and this is the choice of Abu Ubaydah and Abu Hatim. Ya'qub recited ﴿tuqta'a﴾ with a damma on the taa' and a light pronunciation, from the root "qata'a" (to cut).

It is narrated from Ibn Kathir "taqta'a" with a fatha on the taa' and a light pronunciation. ﴿Qulubahum﴾ (their hearts) is in the accusative, meaning that you yourself do that to them. Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash recited: ﴿wa-law qutti'at qulubuhum﴾ (even if their hearts were cut).

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

And others are deferred until Allah's command: that is, delayed, so that He may decide concerning them what He decides.

They are the three who stayed behind and tied themselves to the pillars, and who did not go to great lengths in repentance and apology as Abu Lubabah and his companions did. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was gentle with them, forbade people from speaking to them, and ordered their wives to separate from them, until anxiety overwhelmed them and grief tore them apart. The earth became constricted for them despite its vastness. They had been among the people of Badr, so people began saying, "They are ruined, unless an excuse is revealed for them." Others began saying, "Perhaps Allah will forgive them." They were left waiting for Allah's command, not knowing whether they would be punished or shown mercy, until Allah accepted their repentance after fifty nights and revealed ﴿And [He also turned in forgiveness] to the three who were left behind﴾.

Allah's words: ﴿And those who took a mosque for harm﴾, the verse.

The exegetes said: The Banu Amr ibn Awf built the Mosque of Quba and sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), asking him to come and pray in it. He came and prayed in it. Their brothers, the Banu Ghanm ibn Awf, envied them and said, "We will build a mosque and send to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to pray in it, as he prayed in our brothers' mosque, and Abu Amir al-Nu'man the monk will pray in it when he returns from Syria." Abu Amir was a man from among them; he was the father of Hanzalah, "the one washed by the angels." He had become a monk in the Jahiliyyah, had embraced Christianity, and had worn coarse wool. When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah, Abu Amir said to him, "What is this that you have brought?" He said, "I have brought the Hanifiyyah, the religion of Ibrahim." Abu Amir said, "I am upon it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "You are not upon it." He said, "Yes, but you have introduced into the Hanifiyyah what is not part of it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "I have not done that; rather, I have brought it pure and white." Then he said to the Prophet (ﷺ):

"May Allah cause the liar among us to die, a lone exile."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Amin." He was named "the Fasiq" (the transgressor). When the day of Uhud came, Abu Amir said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "If I find a people who fight you, I will fight you alongside them." He continued fighting him until the day of Hunayn. When Hawazin was defeated, he went out to the Romans seeking support, and he sent to the hypocrites: "Prepare whatever strength and weapons you can, and build me a mosque, for I am going to Caesar, the king of the Romans, to bring an army of Romans to expel Muhammad and his companions." This is Allah's words: ﴿and in preparation for those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger﴾.

So they built a mosque beside the Mosque of Quba. Those who built it were twelve men: Khidham ibn Khalid, from whose house the mosque was taken; Tha'labah ibn Hatib; Mu'tib ibn Qushayr; Abu al-Ara'd; Abbad ibn Hunayf; Harithah ibn Amir; [Jariyah and his two sons] [[The correction is from Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi: 175.]] Mujammi' and Zayd; Nabtal ibn al-Harith; Lahhad ibn Uthman; and Wadi'ah ibn Thabit. Mujammi' ibn Yazid led them in prayer. When they finished, they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was preparing for Tabuk, and said, "O Messenger of Allah, we have built a mosque for the sick, for those in need, for rainy nights and cold nights. We would love for you to come to us, pray in it for us, and invoke blessing." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "I am about to set out on a journey. If we return, Allah willing, we will come to you and pray for you there" [57].

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from Tabuk and stopped at Dhu Awan, a place an hour's distance from Madinah, they asked him to come to their mosque. He called for his garment to wear, intending to go to them, but the Qur'an was revealed to him, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed him about the Mosque of Harm and what they had planned. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned Malik ibn al-Dukhshum, Ma'n ibn Adi, Amir ibn al-Sakan, and al-Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah, and said to them, "Go to this wrongdoing mosque and its people; demolish it and burn it." Abu Amir the monk died in Syria, alone and a stranger. About it Ka'b ibn Malik said:

"Allah forbid, from the deed of the wicked,
like your effort among the clan, O Abd Amr.
As for your claim that you have nobility and palms,
you have sold faith for disbelief."

[[The full story is mentioned in Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, 175; Zad al-Masir: 3/339; and the poem in al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham: 2/424.]]

Ikrimah said: Umar ibn al-Khattab asked one of them, "What did you contribute to this mosque?" He said, "I contributed a pillar." Umar said, "Rejoice in it, around your neck in the Fire of Hell."

It is also narrated that the Banu Amr ibn Awf, who built the Mosque of Quba, asked Umar ibn al-Khattab during his caliphate to permit Mujammi' ibn Harithah to lead them in prayer in their mosque. He said, "No, and no blessing to the eye. Is it not the Mosque of Harm?" Mujammi' said to him, "O Commander of the Faithful, do not hasten against me. By Allah, I prayed in it, and I do not know what they concealed in it. I was a young man who recited the Qur'an, and they were a steadfast people who were eager, and they knew nothing of the Qur'an. So I prayed, and I do not think they were prevented from anything, except that they were humbling themselves before Allah. I did not know what was in their hearts."

He said, "I do not like to pray in it, for it was built on harm. Every mosque built for harm, display, or reputation will ultimately trace back to the Mosque of Harm" [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/36.]].

﴿And disbelief﴾: hypocrisy. ﴿And division among the believers﴾: they divide their community with it, because they used to pray together in the Mosque of Quba. They built the Mosque of Harm so that some of them would pray in it instead of the Mosque of Quba, and some would pray in the Mosque of Quba, so they would disagree and divide because of it. ﴿And in preparation﴾: waiting and readying for ﴿those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger﴾ earlier, namely Abu Amir the monk, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called "the Fasiq," so that he would pray in it when he returned from Syria, and prevail over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

which have become desolate from pilgrimage and from time?"

[[Al-Sihah by al-Jawhari: 6/2209; Lisan al-Arab: 4/170, citing only the first half.]]

Meaning: since the pilgrimage and since time. ﴿More worthy﴾: more deserving that you ﴿stand in it﴾ in prayer. The scholars differed concerning which mosque is ﴿founded on piety﴾. Some said it is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in which are his pulpit and his grave.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us, and al-Abdi informed us: Ahmad ibn Najdah narrated to us, al-Jamani narrated to us, Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from Uthman ibn Abdullah ibn Abi Rafi', from Ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The mosque founded on piety is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is indicated by what was narrated:

Humayd al-Kharrat narrated from Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, that Abd al-Rahman told him that he entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the house of one of his wives. He said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, which mosque is founded on piety?" He took a handful of pebbles and struck them on the ground, then said: "It is your mosque here, the Mosque of Madinah."

Anas ibn Abi Yahya narrated from his father, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: it is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Awfi said: it is the Mosque of Quba. They both came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this, and he said: "It is this one," meaning the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Ibn Yazid, Ibn Zayd, and Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: it is the Mosque of Quba. This is also the narration of Ali ibn Abi Talhah and Atiyyah from Ibn Abbas.

﴿In it are men who love that they purify themselves﴾: from ritual impurities and filth with water. Al-Kalbi said: it is washing the rear with water. Ata' said: they used to cleanse themselves with water and would not sleep at night in a state of major impurity.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the people of Quba when this verse was revealed: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has praised you concerning purification. What is it?" They said: "We cleanse ourselves with water" [[Kanz al-Ummal: 13/7, hadith 33709.]].

﴿And Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾: i.e., those who are purified. The taa' was assimilated into the taa' (ta') because their points of articulation are close.

Yazid ibn Ajrah said: Fever came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the form of a black slave-girl. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her, "Who are you?" She said: "Umm MalDam; I drink blood, eat flesh, yellow the face, and thin the bone."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Then go to the Ansar, for they have rights over us." So fever struck the Ansar.

The next day he said: "What is the matter with the Ansar?" It was said: "They have all been stricken with fever." He said: "Come, let us go and visit them." He visited them and kept saying: "Rejoice, for it is an expiation and a purification" [59].

They said: "O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that it may remain with us for years, so that it may be an expiation for our sins." Then Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾ through fever from their sins, ﴿and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾ from sins.

﴿Is one who founded his building﴾: The readers differed about it. Nafi' and the people of Syria recited ﴿Assisa bunyanuhu﴾ with a damma on the hamza and the nun, in the passive form. Abu Hatim mentioned it from Zayd ibn Thabit. Imarah ibn Sa'id recited ﴿Ā'assa﴾ with a long vowel, a fatha on the sin and the nun, in the pattern of "amana." Likewise the second instance. ﴿Ā'assa, assa, and assasa﴾ have the same meaning; af'ala and fa''ala are close in transitivity.

The rest recited with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the first sin, in the active form, and Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this.

﴿Upon piety from Allah﴾. Isa ibn Umar recited ﴿taqwan min Allah﴾ with tanwin. ﴿And approval is better, or one who founded his building upon the brink﴾: i.e., the edge. Abu Ubayd said: al-shafa is the border, and its dual is al-shafawan.

﴿Of a crumbling cliff﴾: Asim and Hamzah recited it with a light pronunciation, and the rest with a heavy pronunciation; both are dialects. It refers to a well that has not been trodden. Abu Ubaydah said: it is a pit, and what the torrent washes out of the valleys. ﴿Crumbling﴾ (hari): i.e., falling, the one that collapses piece by piece as sand or soft material crumbles. It is said it is an inverted form: its yā' is moved and postponed, so it is said "hār," as one says "shākī al-silāḥ" and "shā'ik al-silāḥ," and "āq" and "ā'iq." The poet said:

"And an obstacle did not prevent me from her love."

It was also said: it is from hāra yahāru, meaning it collapsed, like khāfa yakhāfu. This is an example of the weakness of their intentions and the scarcity of their insight in knowledge. ﴿And it collapsed﴾: it was scattered. It is said: hāra and inhāra and yahūru have the same meaning, meaning it fell and was demolished. From this it is said "tahawwara al-layl" (the night passed) when most of it has gone. In the codex of Ubayy: "and its foundations collapsed with it." ﴿Into the fire of Hell. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

Qatadah said: By Allah, [it did not wait long] before it fell into the Fire. It was mentioned to us that a pit was dug in that place, and they saw smoke coming out of it. Jabir ibn Abdullah said: I saw smoke coming out of the Mosque of Harm. Khalaf ibn Yasin al-Kufi said: I performed Hajj with my father in the time of the Umayyads, and I saw in Madinah the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs, meaning the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Quba, in which is the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis. When the time of Abu Ja'far came, they said: "The ignorant person enters and does not recognize the qiblah." So the building that had been built at the hands of Abd al-Samad ibn Ali was demolished. And I saw the mosque of the hypocrites that Allah, Exalted, mentioned in the Qur'an, and in it was a hole from which smoke comes out, and today it is a rubbish heap [[Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/405.]].

﴿Their building which they built will not cease to be a doubt﴾ in their hearts: doubt and hypocrisy. ﴿In their hearts﴾. They think that by building it they were doing good, just as the calf was made beloved to the people of Musa. Ibn Abbas said: doubt and hypocrisy. Al-Kalbi said: he made it beloved and adorned it, because they claimed they would not follow him. Al-Suddi, Habib, and al-Mubarrad said: because Allah demolished their building, which they built, leaving a rancor in their hearts. ﴿Unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾: their hearts are torn apart so that they die, like His words: ﴿We would have severed from him the aorta﴾ [[Surah al-Haqqah 69:46.]], because life ends when the heart is severed.

Al-Hasan, Ya'qub, and Abu Hatim recited: ﴿ilā an tuqatta'a﴾ with a light pronunciation, meaning "until," as a limit. The interpretation of al-Dahhak and Qatadah supports this: they will remain in doubt until they die, and then they will be certain and will know clearly.

The readers differed about His words ﴿taqatta'a﴾. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Ibn Amir, Hamzah, al-Mufaddal, and Hafs recited ﴿taqatta'a﴾ with a fatha on the taa' and the ta', with a shadda, meaning "taqatta'a," then one of the two taa's was deleted. Yahya ibn Kathir, Mujahid, Nafi', Asim, Abu Amr, and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿tuqatti'a﴾ with a damma on the taa' and a shadda on the ta', in the passive form, and this is the choice of Abu Ubaydah and Abu Hatim. Ya'qub recited ﴿tuqta'a﴾ with a damma on the taa' and a light pronunciation, from the root "qata'a" (to cut).

It is narrated from Ibn Kathir "taqta'a" with a fatha on the taa' and a light pronunciation. ﴿Qulubahum﴾ (their hearts) is in the accusative, meaning that you yourself do that to them. Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash recited: ﴿wa-law qutti'at qulubuhum﴾ (even if their hearts were cut).

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

And others are deferred until Allah's command: that is, delayed, so that He may decide concerning them what He decides.

They are the three who stayed behind and tied themselves to the pillars, and who did not go to great lengths in repentance and apology as Abu Lubabah and his companions did. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was gentle with them, forbade people from speaking to them, and ordered their wives to separate from them, until anxiety overwhelmed them and grief tore them apart. The earth became constricted for them despite its vastness. They had been among the people of Badr, so people began saying, "They are ruined, unless an excuse is revealed for them." Others began saying, "Perhaps Allah will forgive them." They were left waiting for Allah's command, not knowing whether they would be punished or shown mercy, until Allah accepted their repentance after fifty nights and revealed ﴿And [He also turned in forgiveness] to the three who were left behind﴾.

Allah's words: ﴿And those who took a mosque for harm﴾, the verse.

The exegetes said: The Banu Amr ibn Awf built the Mosque of Quba and sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), asking him to come and pray in it. He came and prayed in it. Their brothers, the Banu Ghanm ibn Awf, envied them and said, "We will build a mosque and send to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to pray in it, as he prayed in our brothers' mosque, and Abu Amir al-Nu'man the monk will pray in it when he returns from Syria." Abu Amir was a man from among them; he was the father of Hanzalah, "the one washed by the angels." He had become a monk in the Jahiliyyah, had embraced Christianity, and had worn coarse wool. When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah, Abu Amir said to him, "What is this that you have brought?" He said, "I have brought the Hanifiyyah, the religion of Ibrahim." Abu Amir said, "I am upon it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "You are not upon it." He said, "Yes, but you have introduced into the Hanifiyyah what is not part of it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "I have not done that; rather, I have brought it pure and white." Then he said to the Prophet (ﷺ):

"May Allah cause the liar among us to die, a lone exile."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Amin." He was named "the Fasiq" (the transgressor). When the day of Uhud came, Abu Amir said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "If I find a people who fight you, I will fight you alongside them." He continued fighting him until the day of Hunayn. When Hawazin was defeated, he went out to the Romans seeking support, and he sent to the hypocrites: "Prepare whatever strength and weapons you can, and build me a mosque, for I am going to Caesar, the king of the Romans, to bring an army of Romans to expel Muhammad and his companions." This is Allah's words: ﴿and in preparation for those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger﴾.

So they built a mosque beside the Mosque of Quba. Those who built it were twelve men: Khidham ibn Khalid, from whose house the mosque was taken; Tha'labah ibn Hatib; Mu'tib ibn Qushayr; Abu al-Ara'd; Abbad ibn Hunayf; Harithah ibn Amir; [Jariyah and his two sons] [[The correction is from Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi: 175.]] Mujammi' and Zayd; Nabtal ibn al-Harith; Lahhad ibn Uthman; and Wadi'ah ibn Thabit. Mujammi' ibn Yazid led them in prayer. When they finished, they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was preparing for Tabuk, and said, "O Messenger of Allah, we have built a mosque for the sick, for those in need, for rainy nights and cold nights. We would love for you to come to us, pray in it for us, and invoke blessing." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "I am about to set out on a journey. If we return, Allah willing, we will come to you and pray for you there" [57].

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from Tabuk and stopped at Dhu Awan, a place an hour's distance from Madinah, they asked him to come to their mosque. He called for his garment to wear, intending to go to them, but the Qur'an was revealed to him, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed him about the Mosque of Harm and what they had planned. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned Malik ibn al-Dukhshum, Ma'n ibn Adi, Amir ibn al-Sakan, and al-Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah, and said to them, "Go to this wrongdoing mosque and its people; demolish it and burn it." They went out quickly until they reached Salim ibn Awf. They also came to the family of Malik ibn al-Dukhshum. Malik said to them, "Wait until I bring you fire from my family." He entered his household, took palm fronds, and lit them into fire. Then they went out chanting until they entered the mosque while its people were inside. They burned and demolished it, and its people scattered from it. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that it be made into a dunghill where carrion, filth, and refuse would be thrown. Abu Amir the monk died in Syria, alone and a stranger. About it Ka'b ibn Malik said:

"Allah forbid, from the deed of the wicked,
like your effort among the clan, O Abd Amr.
As for your claim that you have nobility and palms,
you have sold faith for disbelief."

[[The full story is mentioned in Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, 175; Zad al-Masir: 3/339; and the poem in al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham: 2/424.]]

Ikrimah said: Umar ibn al-Khattab asked one of them, "What did you contribute to this mosque?" He said, "I contributed a pillar." Umar said, "Rejoice in it, around your neck in the Fire of Hell."

It is also narrated that the Banu Amr ibn Awf, who built the Mosque of Quba, asked Umar ibn al-Khattab during his caliphate to permit Mujammi' ibn Harithah to lead them in prayer in their mosque. He said, "No, and no blessing to the eye. Is it not the Mosque of Harm?" Mujammi' said to him, "O Commander of the Faithful, do not hasten against me. By Allah, I prayed in it, and I do not know what they concealed in it. I was a young man who recited the Qur'an, and they were a steadfast people who were eager, and they knew nothing of the Qur'an. So I prayed, and I do not think they were prevented from anything, except that they were humbling themselves before Allah. I did not know what was in their hearts."

Umar accepted his excuse, believed him, and ordered him to pray in the Mosque of Quba.

This is the story of the Mosque of Harm in which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed ﴿And those who took a mosque﴾. The common readers recited it with the wa (and), while the people of Madinah and Syria recited it without the wa. It is also so in the codices of the people of Madinah and Syria.

Ata' said: When Allah granted Umar ibn al-Khattab the conquest of the cities, he ordered the Muslims to build mosques and ordered them not to make two mosques in one city, one adjacent to the other.

Layth narrated that Shaqiq did not attend prayer in the mosque of Banu Amir. It was said to him, "The mosque of Banu so-and-so, they have not prayed in it yet." He said, "I do not like to pray in it, for it was built on harm. Every mosque built for harm, display, or reputation will ultimately trace back to the Mosque of Harm" [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/36.]].

﴿And disbelief﴾: hypocrisy. ﴿And division among the believers﴾: they divide their community with it, because they used to pray together in the Mosque of Quba. They built the Mosque of Harm so that some of them would pray in it instead of the Mosque of Quba, and some would pray in the Mosque of Quba, so they would disagree and divide because of it. ﴿And in preparation﴾: waiting and readying for ﴿those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger﴾ earlier, namely Abu Amir the monk, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called "the Fasiq," so that he would pray in it when he returned from Syria, and prevail over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Al-A'mash recited: ﴿wa-irsadan lil-ladhina harabu Allah﴾ (for those who warred against Allah). ﴿And they will swear, "We intended only the good"﴾: they intended only the good deed, which was for the sick among the Muslims, the extension of relief for the weak and the ill, and those unable to travel to the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿And Allah testifies that they are liars﴾ in their words and oaths. Then He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Do not stand in it ever﴾.

﴿Indeed, a mosque founded on piety﴾: the lam here is the lam of initiation and oath, meaning "By Allah, indeed a mosque..." ﴿was founded on piety﴾: its foundation was laid and its construction began. ﴿From the first day﴾: from the first day it was built. It was said that the meaning is: since the first day its foundation was laid. Al-Mubarrad said: It was said concerning the meaning of the phrase "min hajj wa-amn dahr" (from pilgrimage and security through time), i.e., "the one who is pilgrimage and security throughout time." Zuhayr composed:

"To whom belong the abodes at the Qunnat al-Hijr,
which have become desolate from pilgrimage and from time?"

[[Al-Sihah by al-Jawhari: 6/2209; Lisan al-Arab: 4/170, citing only the first half.]]

Meaning: since the pilgrimage and since time. ﴿More worthy﴾: more deserving that you ﴿stand in it﴾ in prayer. The scholars differed concerning which mosque is ﴿founded on piety﴾. Some said it is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in which are his pulpit and his grave.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us, and al-Abdi informed us: Ahmad ibn Najdah narrated to us, al-Jamani narrated to us, Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from Uthman ibn Abdullah ibn Abi Rafi', from Ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The mosque founded on piety is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is indicated by what was narrated:

Humayd al-Kharrat narrated from Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, that Abd al-Rahman told him that he entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the house of one of his wives. He said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, which mosque is founded on piety?" He took a handful of pebbles and struck them on the ground, then said: "It is your mosque here, the Mosque of Madinah."

Anas ibn Abi Yahya narrated from his father, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: it is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Awfi said: it is the Mosque of Quba. They both came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this, and he said: "It is this one," meaning the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Ibn Yazid, Ibn Zayd, and Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: it is the Mosque of Quba. This is also the narration of Ali ibn Abi Talhah and Atiyyah from Ibn Abbas.

﴿In it are men who love that they purify themselves﴾: from ritual impurities and filth with water. Al-Kalbi said: it is washing the rear with water. Ata' said: they used to cleanse themselves with water and would not sleep at night in a state of major impurity.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the people of Quba when this verse was revealed: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has praised you concerning purification. What is it?" They said: "We cleanse ourselves with water" [[Kanz al-Ummal: 13/7, hadith 33709.]].

﴿And Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾: i.e., those who are purified. The taa' was assimilated into the taa' (ta') because their points of articulation are close.

Yazid ibn Ajrah said: Fever came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the form of a black slave-girl. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her, "Who are you?" She said: "Umm MalDam; I drink blood, eat flesh, yellow the face, and thin the bone."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Then go to the Ansar, for they have rights over us." So fever struck the Ansar.

The next day he said: "What is the matter with the Ansar?" It was said: "They have all been stricken with fever." He said: "Come, let us go and visit them." He visited them and kept saying: "Rejoice, for it is an expiation and a purification" [59].

They said: "O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that it may remain with us for years, so that it may be an expiation for our sins." Then Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾ through fever from their sins, ﴿and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾ from sins.

﴿Is one who founded his building﴾: The readers differed about it. Nafi' and the people of Syria recited ﴿Assisa bunyanuhu﴾ with a damma on the hamza and the nun, in the passive form. Abu Hatim mentioned it from Zayd ibn Thabit. Imarah ibn Sa'id recited ﴿Ā'assa﴾ with a long vowel, a fatha on the sin and the nun, in the pattern of "amana." Likewise the second instance. ﴿Ā'assa, assa, and assasa﴾ have the same meaning; af'ala and fa''ala are close in transitivity.

The rest recited with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the first sin, in the active form, and Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this.

﴿Upon piety from Allah﴾. Isa ibn Umar recited ﴿taqwan min Allah﴾ with tanwin. ﴿And approval is better, or one who founded his building upon the brink﴾: i.e., the edge. Abu Ubayd said: al-shafa is the border, and its dual is al-shafawan.

﴿Of a crumbling cliff﴾: Asim and Hamzah recited it with a light pronunciation, and the rest with a heavy pronunciation; both are dialects. It refers to a well that has not been trodden. Abu Ubaydah said: it is a pit, and what the torrent washes out of the valleys. ﴿Crumbling﴾ (hari): i.e., falling, the one that collapses piece by piece as sand or soft material crumbles. It is said it is an inverted form: its yā' is moved and postponed, so it is said "hār," as one says "shākī al-silāḥ" and "shā'ik al-silāḥ," and "āq" and "ā'iq." The poet said:

"And an obstacle did not prevent me from her love."

It was also said: it is from hāra yahāru, meaning it collapsed, like khāfa yakhāfu. This is an example of the weakness of their intentions and the scarcity of their insight in knowledge. ﴿And it collapsed﴾: it was scattered. It is said: hāra and inhāra and yahūru have the same meaning, meaning it fell and was demolished. From this it is said "tahawwara al-layl" (the night passed) when most of it has gone. In the codex of Ubayy: "and its foundations collapsed with it." ﴿Into the fire of Hell. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

Qatadah said: By Allah, [it did not wait long] before it fell into the Fire. It was mentioned to us that a pit was dug in that place, and they saw smoke coming out of it. Jabir ibn Abdullah said: I saw smoke coming out of the Mosque of Harm. Khalaf ibn Yasin al-Kufi said: I performed Hajj with my father in the time of the Umayyads, and I saw in Madinah the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs, meaning the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Quba, in which is the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis. When the time of Abu Ja'far came, they said: "The ignorant person enters and does not recognize the qiblah." So the building that had been built at the hands of Abd al-Samad ibn Ali was demolished. And I saw the mosque of the hypocrites that Allah, Exalted, mentioned in the Qur'an, and in it was a hole from which smoke comes out, and today it is a rubbish heap [[Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/405.]].

﴿Their building which they built will not cease to be a doubt﴾ in their hearts: doubt and hypocrisy. ﴿In their hearts﴾. They think that by building it they were doing good, just as the calf was made beloved to the people of Musa. Ibn Abbas said: doubt and hypocrisy. Al-Kalbi said: he made it beloved and adorned it, because they claimed they would not follow him. Al-Suddi, Habib, and al-Mubarrad said: because Allah demolished their building, which they built, leaving a rancor in their hearts. ﴿Unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾: their hearts are torn apart so that they die, like His words: ﴿We would have severed from him the aorta﴾ [[Surah al-Haqqah 69:46.]], because life ends when the heart is severed.

Al-Hasan, Ya'qub, and Abu Hatim recited: ﴿ilā an tuqatta'a﴾ with a light pronunciation, meaning "until," as a limit. The interpretation of al-Dahhak and Qatadah supports this: they will remain in doubt until they die, and then they will be certain and will know clearly.

The readers differed about His words ﴿taqatta'a﴾. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Ibn Amir, Hamzah, al-Mufaddal, and Hafs recited ﴿taqatta'a﴾ with a fatha on the taa' and the ta', with a shadda, meaning "taqatta'a," then one of the two taa's was deleted. Yahya ibn Kathir, Mujahid, Nafi', Asim, Abu Amr, and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿tuqatti'a﴾ with a damma on the taa' and a shadda on the ta', in the passive form, and this is the choice of Abu Ubaydah and Abu Hatim. Ya'qub recited ﴿tuqta'a﴾ with a damma on the taa' and a light pronunciation, from the root "qata'a" (to cut).

It is narrated from Ibn Kathir "taqta'a" with a fatha on the taa' and a light pronunciation. ﴿Qulubahum﴾ (their hearts) is in the accusative, meaning that you yourself do that to them. Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash recited: ﴿wa-law qutti'at qulubuhum﴾ (even if their hearts were cut).

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

And others are deferred until Allah's command: that is, delayed, so that He may decide concerning them what He decides.

They are the three who stayed behind and tied themselves to the pillars, and who did not go to great lengths in repentance and apology as Abu Lubabah and his companions did. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was gentle with them, forbade people from speaking to them, and ordered their wives to separate from them, until anxiety overwhelmed them and grief tore them apart. The earth became constricted for them despite its vastness. They had been among the people of Badr, so people began saying, "They are ruined, unless an excuse is revealed for them." Others began saying, "Perhaps Allah will forgive them." They were left waiting for Allah's command, not knowing whether they would be punished or shown mercy, until Allah accepted their repentance after fifty nights and revealed ﴿And [He also turned in forgiveness] to the three who were left behind﴾.

Allah's words: ﴿And those who took a mosque for harm﴾, the verse.

The exegetes said: The Banu Amr ibn Awf built the Mosque of Quba and sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), asking him to come and pray in it. He came and prayed in it. Their brothers, the Banu Ghanm ibn Awf, envied them and said, "We will build a mosque and send to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to pray in it, as he prayed in our brothers' mosque, and Abu Amir al-Nu'man the monk will pray in it when he returns from Syria." Abu Amir was a man from among them; he was the father of Hanzalah, "the one washed by the angels." He had become a monk in the Jahiliyyah, had embraced Christianity, and had worn coarse wool. When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah, Abu Amir said to him, "What is this that you have brought?" He said, "I have brought the Hanifiyyah, the religion of Ibrahim." Abu Amir said, "I am upon it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "You are not upon it." He said, "Yes, but you have introduced into the Hanifiyyah what is not part of it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "I have not done that; rather, I have brought it pure and white." Then he said to the Prophet (ﷺ):

"May Allah cause the liar among us to die, a lone exile."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Amin." He was named "the Fasiq" (the transgressor). When the day of Uhud came, Abu Amir said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "If I find a people who fight you, I will fight you alongside them." He continued fighting him until the day of Hunayn. When Hawazin was defeated, he went out to the Romans seeking support, and he sent to the hypocrites: "Prepare whatever strength and weapons you can, and build me a mosque, for I am going to Caesar, the king of the Romans, to bring an army of Romans to expel Muhammad and his companions." This is Allah's words: ﴿and in preparation for those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger﴾.

So they built a mosque beside the Mosque of Quba. Those who built it were twelve men: Khidham ibn Khalid, from whose house the mosque was taken; Tha'labah ibn Hatib; Mu'tib ibn Qushayr; Abu al-Ara'd; Abbad ibn Hunayf; Harithah ibn Amir; [Jariyah and his two sons] [[The correction is from Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi: 175.]] Mujammi' and Zayd; Nabtal ibn al-Harith; Lahhad ibn Uthman; and Wadi'ah ibn Thabit. Mujammi' ibn Yazid led them in prayer. When they finished, they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was preparing for Tabuk, and said, "O Messenger of Allah, we have built a mosque for the sick, for those in need, for rainy nights and cold nights. We would love for you to come to us, pray in it for us, and invoke blessing." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "I am about to set out on a journey. If we return, Allah willing, we will come to you and pray for you there" [57].

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from Tabuk and stopped at Dhu Awan, a place an hour's distance from Madinah, they asked him to come to their mosque. He called for his garment to wear, intending to go to them, but the Qur'an was revealed to him, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed him about the Mosque of Harm and what they had planned. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned Malik ibn al-Dukhshum, Ma'n ibn Adi, Amir ibn al-Sakan, and al-Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah, and said to them, "Go to this wrongdoing mosque and its people; demolish it and burn it." They went out quickly until they reached Salim ibn Awf. They also came to the family of Malik ibn al-Dukhshum. Malik said to them, "Wait until I bring you fire from my family." He entered his household, took palm fronds, and lit them into fire. Then they went out chanting until they entered the mosque while its people were inside. They burned and demolished it, and its people scattered from it. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that it be made into a dunghill where carrion, filth, and refuse would be thrown. Abu Amir the monk died in Syria, alone and a stranger. About it Ka'b ibn Malik said:

"Allah forbid, from the deed of the wicked,
like your effort among the clan, O Abd Amr.
As for your claim that you have nobility and palms,
you have sold faith for disbelief."

[[The full story is mentioned in Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, 175; Zad al-Masir: 3/339; and the poem in al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham: 2/424.]]

Ikrimah said: Umar ibn al-Khattab asked one of them, "What did you contribute to this mosque?" He said, "I contributed a pillar." Umar said, "Rejoice in it, around your neck in the Fire of Hell."

It is also narrated that the Banu Amr ibn Awf, who built the Mosque of Quba, asked Umar ibn al-Khattab during his caliphate to permit Mujammi' ibn Harithah to lead them in prayer in their mosque. He said, "No, and no blessing to the eye. Is it not the Mosque of Harm?" Mujammi' said to him, "O Commander of the Faithful, do not hasten against me. By Allah, I prayed in it, and I do not know what they concealed in it. I was a young man who recited the Qur'an, and they were a steadfast people who were eager, and they knew nothing of the Qur'an. So I prayed, and I do not think they were prevented from anything, except that they were humbling themselves before Allah. I did not know what was in their hearts."

Umar accepted his excuse, believed him, and ordered him to pray in the Mosque of Quba.

This is the story of the Mosque of Harm in which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed ﴿And those who took a mosque﴾. The common readers recited it with the wa (and), while the people of Madinah and Syria recited it without the wa. It is also so in the codices of the people of Madinah and Syria.

Ata' said: When Allah granted Umar ibn al-Khattab the conquest of the cities, he ordered the Muslims to build mosques and ordered them not to make two mosques in one city, one adjacent to the other.

Layth narrated that Shaqiq did not attend prayer in the mosque of Banu Amir. It was said to him, "The mosque of Banu so-and-so, they have not prayed in it yet." He said, "I do not like to pray in it, for it was built on harm. Every mosque built for harm, display, or reputation will ultimately trace back to the Mosque of Harm" [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 11/36.]].

﴿And disbelief﴾: hypocrisy. ﴿And division among the believers﴾: they divide their community with it, because they used to pray together in the Mosque of Quba. They built the Mosque of Harm so that some of them would pray in it instead of the Mosque of Quba, and some would pray in the Mosque of Quba, so they would disagree and divide because of it. ﴿And in preparation﴾: waiting and readying for ﴿those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger﴾ earlier, namely Abu Amir the monk, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called "the Fasiq," so that he would pray in it when he returned from Syria, and prevail over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Al-A'mash recited: ﴿wa-irsadan lil-ladhina harabu Allah﴾ (for those who warred against Allah). ﴿And they will swear, "We intended only the good"﴾: they intended only the good deed, which was for the sick among the Muslims, the extension of relief for the weak and the ill, and those unable to travel to the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿And Allah testifies that they are liars﴾ in their words and oaths. Then He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Do not stand in it ever﴾.

﴿Indeed, a mosque founded on piety﴾: the lam here is the lam of initiation and oath, meaning "By Allah, indeed a mosque..." ﴿was founded on piety﴾: its foundation was laid and its construction began. ﴿From the first day﴾: from the first day it was built. It was said that the meaning is: since the first day its foundation was laid. Al-Mubarrad said: It was said concerning the meaning of the phrase "min hajj wa-amn dahr" (from pilgrimage and security through time), i.e., "the one who is pilgrimage and security throughout time." Zuhayr composed:

"To whom belong the abodes at the Qunnat al-Hijr,
which have become desolate from pilgrimage and from time?"

[[Al-Sihah by al-Jawhari: 6/2209; Lisan al-Arab: 4/170, citing only the first half.]]

Meaning: since the pilgrimage and since time. ﴿More worthy﴾: more deserving that you ﴿stand in it﴾ in prayer. The scholars differed concerning which mosque is ﴿founded on piety﴾. Some said it is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in which are his pulpit and his grave.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us, and al-Abdi informed us: Ahmad ibn Najdah narrated to us, al-Jamani narrated to us, Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from Uthman ibn Abdullah ibn Abi Rafi', from Ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The mosque founded on piety is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is indicated by what was narrated:

Humayd al-Kharrat narrated from Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, that Abd al-Rahman told him that he entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the house of one of his wives. He said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, which mosque is founded on piety?" He took a handful of pebbles and struck them on the ground, then said: "It is your mosque here, the Mosque of Madinah."

Anas ibn Abi Yahya narrated from his father, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: it is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Awfi said: it is the Mosque of Quba. They both came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this, and he said: "It is this one," meaning the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Ibn Yazid, Ibn Zayd, and Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: it is the Mosque of Quba. This is also the narration of Ali ibn Abi Talhah and Atiyyah from Ibn Abbas.

﴿In it are men who love that they purify themselves﴾: from ritual impurities and filth with water. Al-Kalbi said: it is washing the rear with water. Ata' said: they used to cleanse themselves with water and would not sleep at night in a state of major impurity.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the people of Quba when this verse was revealed: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has praised you concerning purification. What is it?" They said: "We cleanse ourselves with water" [[Kanz al-Ummal: 13/7, hadith 33709.]].

﴿And Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾: i.e., those who are purified. The taa' was assimilated into the taa' (ta') because their points of articulation are close.

Yazid ibn Ajrah said: Fever came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the form of a black slave-girl. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her, "Who are you?" She said: "Umm MalDam; I drink blood, eat flesh, yellow the face, and thin the bone."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Then go to the Ansar, for they have rights over us." So fever struck the Ansar.

The next day he said: "What is the matter with the Ansar?" It was said: "They have all been stricken with fever." He said: "Come, let us go and visit them." He visited them and kept saying: "Rejoice, for it is an expiation and a purification" [59].

They said: "O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that it may remain with us for years, so that it may be an expiation for our sins." Then Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾ through fever from their sins, ﴿and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾ from sins.

﴿Is one who founded his building﴾: The readers differed about it. Nafi' and the people of Syria recited ﴿Assisa bunyanuhu﴾ with a damma on the hamza and the nun, in the passive form. Abu Hatim mentioned it from Zayd ibn Thabit. Imarah ibn Sa'id recited ﴿Ā'assa﴾ with a long vowel, a fatha on the sin and the nun, in the pattern of "amana." Likewise the second instance. ﴿Ā'assa, assa, and assasa﴾ have the same meaning; af'ala and fa''ala are close in transitivity.

The rest recited with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the first sin, in the active form, and Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this.

﴿Upon piety from Allah﴾. Isa ibn Umar recited ﴿taqwan min Allah﴾ with tanwin. ﴿And approval is better, or one who founded his building upon the brink﴾: i.e., the edge. Abu Ubayd said: al-shafa is the border, and its dual is al-shafawan.

﴿Of a crumbling cliff﴾: Asim and Hamzah recited it with a light pronunciation, and the rest with a heavy pronunciation; both are dialects. It refers to a well that has not been trodden. Abu Ubaydah said: it is a pit, and what the torrent washes out of the valleys. ﴿Crumbling﴾ (hari): i.e., falling, the one that collapses piece by piece as sand or soft material crumbles. It is said it is an inverted form: its yā' is moved and postponed, so it is said "hār," as one says "shākī al-silāḥ" and "shā'ik al-silāḥ," and "āq" and "ā'iq." The poet said:

"And an obstacle did not prevent me from her love."

It was also said: it is from hāra yahāru, meaning it collapsed, like khāfa yakhāfu. This is an example of the weakness of their intentions and the scarcity of their insight in knowledge. ﴿And it collapsed﴾: it was scattered. It is said: hāra and inhāra and yahūru have the same meaning, meaning it fell and was demolished. From this it is said "tahawwara al-layl" (the night passed) when most of it has gone. In the codex of Ubayy: "and its foundations collapsed with it." ﴿Into the fire of Hell. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

Qatadah said: By Allah, [it did not wait long] before it fell into the Fire. It was mentioned to us that a pit was dug in that place, and they saw smoke coming out of it. Jabir ibn Abdullah said: I saw smoke coming out of the Mosque of Harm. Khalaf ibn Yasin al-Kufi said: I performed Hajj with my father in the time of the Umayyads, and I saw in Madinah the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs, meaning the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Quba, in which is the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis. When the time of Abu Ja'far came, they said: "The ignorant person enters and does not recognize the qiblah." So the building that had been built at the hands of Abd al-Samad ibn Ali was demolished. And I saw the mosque of the hypocrites that Allah, Exalted, mentioned in the Qur'an, and in it was a hole from which smoke comes out, and today it is a rubbish heap [[Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/405.]].

﴿Their building which they built will not cease to be a doubt﴾ in their hearts: doubt and hypocrisy. ﴿In their hearts﴾. They think that by building it they were doing good, just as the calf was made beloved to the people of Musa. Ibn Abbas said: doubt and hypocrisy. Al-Kalbi said: he made it beloved and adorned it, because they claimed they would not follow him. Al-Suddi, Habib, and al-Mubarrad said: because Allah demolished their building, which they built, leaving a rancor in their hearts. ﴿Unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾: their hearts are torn apart so that they die, like His words: ﴿We would have severed from him the aorta﴾ [[Surah al-Haqqah 69:46.]], because life ends when the heart is severed.

Al-Hasan, Ya'qub, and Abu Hatim recited: ﴿ilā an tuqatta'a﴾ with a light pronunciation, meaning "until," as a limit. The interpretation of al-Dahhak and Qatadah supports this: they will remain in doubt until they die, and then they will be certain and will know clearly.

The readers differed about His words ﴿taqatta'a﴾. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Ibn Amir, Hamzah, al-Mufaddal, and Hafs recited ﴿taqatta'a﴾ with a fatha on the taa' and the ta', with a shadda, meaning "taqatta'a," then one of the two taa's was deleted. Yahya ibn Kathir, Mujahid, Nafi', Asim, Abu Amr, and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿tuqatti'a﴾ with a damma on the taa' and a shadda on the ta', in the passive form, and this is the choice of Abu Ubaydah and Abu Hatim. Ya'qub recited ﴿tuqta'a﴾ with a damma on the taa' and a light pronunciation, from the root "qata'a" (to cut).

It is narrated from Ibn Kathir "taqta'a" with a fatha on the taa' and a light pronunciation. ﴿Qulubahum﴾ (their hearts) is in the accusative, meaning that you yourself do that to them. Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash recited: ﴿wa-law qutti'at qulubuhum﴾ (even if their hearts were cut).

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 9, verse 111–114 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties.﴾

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: When the Ansar pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of al-'Aqaba in Makkah, they were seventy souls. Abdullah ibn Rawaha said: "O Messenger of Allah, stipulate for your Lord and for yourself whatever you wish." He said: "I stipulate for my Lord that you worship Him and associate nothing with Him, and I stipulate for myself that you protect me from what you protect yourselves and your properties from." They said: "If we do that, what will we have?" He said: "Paradise." [60] [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 11/49.]]

Al-A'mash said: "Paradise." It is also the reading of Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him): ﴿they fight in the cause of Allah, so they kill and are killed﴾. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with the object preceding the subject, in the sense that some of them are killed and the rest kill; the others read it with the subject preceding the object. ﴿A promise﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun, ﴿binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an﴾. Then He congratulated them, the Mighty One, the Majestic, saying:
﴿So rejoice in your transaction which you have made, and that is the great triumph.﴾ Qatadah said: "He was the most expensive of their price." al-Hasan said: "Hear of a profitable transaction which Allah made with every believer. By Allah, there is not a believer on the face of the earth except that he has entered into this transaction."

He said: A Bedouin passed by the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was reciting this verse, and said: "Whose speech is this?" He said: "It is the speech of Allah." He said: "By Allah, it is a profitable transaction; we will neither cancel it nor ask for its cancellation." So he went out to the military expedition and was martyred. [[See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 8/268.]]

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Habibi recited to us. He said: Abu al-Hasan al-Aqili recited to us. Bishr ibn Musa al-Asadi recited to us. al-Asma'i recited to me, from Ja'far al-Sadiq (may Allah be pleased with him):

"Shall I sell the precious soul to its Lord? For among all creatures there is no price for it.
By it Paradises are purchased, if I sell it for something other than it; that would indeed be a loss.
If I lose my soul for a worldly thing I have obtained, then the world is lost and the price is lost too." [[Cf. Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 8/268, where the last hemistich is instead: "Indeed my soul is lost and the price is lost too."]]

Al-Sadiq used to say: "O you whose soul has no value, indeed your bodies have no price except Paradise, so do not sell them except for it."

Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi recited to us. al-Qadi Abu al-Rabi' Muhammad ibn Ali recited to us. Abu Ali al-Hasan ibn Asim al-Kufi recited to us:

"Whoever desires a lofty dome in Eden, high in the shade of Tuba, its structures elevated;
its price is the Chosen One, and by Allah He has sold it, so whoever wishes, and Jibril is calling to it."

Then He described them, saying: ﴿the repentant﴾, i.e., they are the repentant. Ibn Mas'ud read "al-ta'ibin al-'abidin" with the final word in the accusative. The commentators said: they repented from polytheism and were cleared of hypocrisy. ﴿The worshippers﴾: those who obey, who devoted sincere worship and testimony.

al-Hasan and Qatadah said: They are a people who made their bodies a means of worship in their night and day, worshipping Allah at all times, in ease and in hardship. ﴿The praisers﴾: those who praise Allah in every state and for every blessing. ﴿The wanderers﴾: the fasting ones.

al-A'mash reported from Abu Salih from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The wanderers are the fasting ones." [61] [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 11/52.]]

Shayban ibn Abd al-Rahman reported from al-Ash'ath who said: I asked Sa'id ibn Jubayr about "the wanderers," and he said:
"They are the fasting ones. Do you not see that when Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentions the fasting ones, He does not mention the wanderers, and when He mentions the wanderers, He does not mention the fasting ones?"

Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: "Indeed the fasting person is a wanderer, for he abandons all pleasures: food, drink and intercourse."

A poet said regarding fasting:
"You see him praying through his night and day, ever abundant in the remembrance of Allah, a wanderer."  [[Fath al-Qadir: 2/408.]]

al-Hasan said: "The wanderers are those who fast from what is lawful and refrain from what is unlawful. By Allah, here there are people whom we have seen fasting from what is lawful but not refraining from what is unlawful; Allah is displeased with them." 'Ata' said: "The wanderers are the warriors and the strivers." It is reported from Amr ibn Nafi' who said: I heard Ikrimah, when asked about the words of Allah the Exalted, "the wanderers," say: "They are the seekers of knowledge." ﴿The bowers, the prostrators﴾: meaning those who pray. ﴿Those who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾. Bassam ibn Abdullah said: "The right is the Sunnah and the wrong is innovation."

﴿And those who guard the limits of Allah﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "Those who keep to the obedience of Allah." al-Hasan said: "The people who fulfil the pledge of Allah." ﴿And give good tidings to the believers.﴾

﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists...﴾ the verse. The scholars differed concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse.
